column2: Your organization has multiple GKE clusters across different projects and wants centralized visibility into container threats, including cryptomining, privilege escalation, and malicious code execution. You have Security Command Center Premium tier enabled. Where should you navigate in the Google Cloud console to view a summary of the top threats affecting your GKE workloads grouped by severity and category?
column3: Security Command Center Findings page, filtered by Container Threat Detection.
column4: GKE Security Posture dashboard, in the Top threats pane.
column5: GKE Workloads page, in the Security tab under each deployment.
column6: Cloud Logging Logs Explorer, filtered by GKE cluster resource type.
column8: When Security Command Center Premium or Enterprise tier is activated, the GKE security posture dashboard shows the Top threats pane that summarizes threats affecting GKE workloads, grouped by severity and category. This pane displays threats such as cryptomining, privilege escalation, and malicious code execution detected by Container Threat Detection. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/about-security-posture-dashboard

column2: Your security team is investigating a suspected service account impersonation attack. A user may have obtained short-lived credentials to perform unauthorized actions as a privileged service account. You need to identify the original user who initiated the impersonation chain in Cloud Audit Logs. Which field in the audit log entry should you examine?
column3: The serviceAccountDelegationInfo field in protoPayload.authenticationInfo
column4: The principalEmail field in protoPayload.authenticationInfo
column5: The authorizationInfo field in protoPayload
column6: The callerIp field in protoPayload.requestMetadata
column8: The serviceAccountDelegationInfo field in Cloud Audit Logs contains the identity delegation history of an authenticated service account, including the firstPartyPrincipal field that shows the original user who created the short-lived credentials for impersonation. This field is essential for tracing back to the actual attacker. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/audit-logging/examples-service-accounts

column2: You are configuring a BigQuery-based threat hunting solution to detect data exfiltration attempts. You need to query BigQuery audit logs to identify jobs that copied data to destination tables outside your organization's project. Which protoPayload field should you primarily analyze to identify potential cross-project data transfers?
column3: Query the protoPayload.response.destinationTable field to identify where query results were stored after job completion.
column4: Query the protoPayload.serviceData.jobInsertRequest.resource.jobConfiguration.query.destinationTable field for all query job destination information.
column5: Query the protoPayload.metadata.jobChange.job.jobConfig.queryConfig.destinationTable field to identify the destination project for query job results.
column6: Query the protoPayload.resourceName field to extract the destination table information from the resource hierarchy path.
column8: The BigQueryAuditMetadata format stores destination table information in the protoPayload.metadata structure. The destinationTable field contains the project, dataset, and table identifiers, allowing you to detect when query results are written to external projects. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/auditlogs

column2: Your organization uses Google Security Operations (SecOps) with Advanced BigQuery Export enabled. After receiving new threat intelligence about a campaign targeting your industry, you need to search for matching IOCs in your historical security telemetry. Which BigQuery table should you query to find artifacts that have already been matched against existing IOC feeds?
column3: Query the ioc_matches table in the secops_linked_data dataset to find artifacts from events that match IOC feeds.
column4: Query the rule_detections table to find all detection matches and filter for IOC-related rule names.
column5: Export logs directly from Cloud Logging to a custom BigQuery dataset and create your own IOC matching queries.
column6: Query the events table in the secops_linked_data dataset and manually search for IOC values using CONTAINS_SUBSTR functions.
column8: The ioc_matches table in the Advanced BigQuery Export dataset stores IOC matches found against UDM events. This table contains artifacts such as domains and IP addresses from events that have already been correlated with ingested IOC feeds, making it the appropriate source for finding historical IOC matches in your security telemetry. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/reports/bigquery-export

column2: Your security team needs to prioritize the remediation of thousands of vulnerability findings in Security Command Center. You want to focus on vulnerabilities that pose the greatest actual risk to your organization's critical assets. Which approach should you use to identify and prioritize the highest-risk findings?
column3: Sort findings by attack exposure score and prioritize remediation of findings with the highest scores that expose your designated high-value resources.
column4: Filter findings by CRITICAL severity level and remediate all critical findings before addressing findings of lower severity.
column5: Use the Compliance page to prioritize findings that violate the most regulatory controls across your applicable security standards.
column6: Export all findings to BigQuery and create a custom scoring algorithm based on CVSS scores and finding age.
column8: Attack exposure scores measure how much a detected security issue exposes high-value resources to potential cyberattacks. Security Command Center's Risk Engine calculates these scores based on simulated attack paths, considering the priority values assigned to high-value resources, the number of attack paths, and the likelihood of successful attacks. This provides context-aware prioritization based on actual risk. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/attack-exposure-learn

column2: A detection engineer at your organization received a CISA advisory about a new ransomware campaign targeting your industry. The engineer needs to assess whether the current Google Security Operations (SecOps) detection rules can identify the specific tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) used by this threat. What should the engineer use to identify gaps in detection coverage against the MITRE ATT&CK framework?
column3: Create a custom dashboard with filters for MITRE technique IDs to correlate advisory TTPs with historical detections.
column4: Navigate to Detection > Rules & Detections and access the MITRE ATT&CK Matrix tab to view coverage by technique and identify gaps.
column5: Open the Curated Detections dashboard and review rule sets mapped to MITRE tactics and techniques mentioned in the advisory.
column6: Run a retrohunt against historical logs using YARA-L rules that match the specific TTPs described in the CISA advisory.
column8: The MITRE ATT&CK matrix dashboard in Google SecOps helps understand your organization's security posture against the MITRE ATT&CK framework. It displays tactics as columns and techniques as cards that are color-coded to indicate detection coverage status. Engineers can search for specific techniques by name or ID mentioned in advisories and identify techniques showing 'No Coverage'. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/mitre-dashboard

column2: Your security team has identified a critical malware incident where a compromised container image was deployed to several GKE clusters in your organization. You need to immediately prevent any further deployments of the malicious image while your team investigates. You want to use the most effective containment approach. What should you do?
column3: Enable Binary Authorization continuous validation on all clusters and configure it to monitor for the malicious image digest.
column4: Update the Binary Authorization policy's defaultAdmissionRule to ALWAYS_DENY and add only verified safe images to the admissionWhitelistPatterns.
column5: Delete the compromised container image from Artifact Registry and revoke all attestations associated with that image digest.
column6: Cordon and drain the affected GKE nodes, then manually delete the Pods running the compromised image from all clusters.
column8: Updating the Binary Authorization policy to ALWAYS_DENY immediately blocks all container deployments that are not explicitly whitelisted. By adding only verified safe images to admissionWhitelistPatterns, you can contain the incident by ensuring no malicious images can be deployed while allowing business-critical operations to continue with known-good images. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/configure-policy-gke

column2: Your organization needs to implement continuous monitoring of Google Cloud resource configurations across multiple projects to detect unauthorized changes to firewall rules and IAM policies. You want to receive notifications in near real-time when these changes occur. What should you do?
column3: Create a Cloud Asset Inventory feed that specifies firewall and IAM policy asset types, and configure it to publish changes to a Pub/Sub topic.
column4: Configure Cloud Logging export sinks to filter and route Admin Activity audit logs for firewall and IAM changes to Pub/Sub.
column5: Enable Security Command Center and configure continuous exports to Pub/Sub with filters for firewall and IAM findings only.
column6: Schedule a recurring Cloud Function that calls the Cloud Asset Inventory ListAssets API every minute and compares results against a baseline stored in Cloud Storage.
column8: Cloud Asset Inventory feeds allow you to receive real-time notifications about resource and policy changes by creating and subscribing to a feed. You can specify asset types such as firewall rules and IAM policies, and notifications are published to a Pub/Sub topic. This is the recommended approach for continuous monitoring. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/asset-inventory/docs/monitor-asset-changes

column2: You are configuring centralized log collection for threat detection across your Google Cloud organization. You need to route all Data Access audit logs from all projects to a single BigQuery dataset for security analytics and threat hunting. Which configuration approach should you use?
column3: Create project-level sinks in each project with identical filters targeting a shared BigQuery dataset in the security project.
column4: Configure the _Default sink at the organization level to route Data Access logs directly to BigQuery by modifying the sink filter.
column5: Create an intercepting aggregated sink at the organization level with the filter LOG_ID('cloudaudit.googleapis.com/data_access') and route to a log bucket with a linked BigQuery dataset.
column6: Create a non-intercepting aggregated sink at the organization level with the filter LOG_ID('cloudaudit.googleapis.com/data_access') and set the destination to a BigQuery dataset in a centralized security project.
column8: Non-intercepting aggregated sinks route log entries from the organization and all child resources to a central destination while maintaining visibility in source projects. The LOG_ID filter correctly targets Data Access audit logs for centralized security analytics. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/aggregated_sinks

column2: Your organization wants to automate the remediation of Security Command Center findings by triggering Cloud Functions when specific vulnerabilities are detected. You need to configure Security Command Center to send findings to a Pub/Sub topic that will trigger the Cloud Functions. What should you configure first?
column3: Create an Event Threat Detection custom module that includes the remediation logic within the detector configuration.
column4: Deploy a Cloud Function with an HTTP trigger and configure Security Command Center to call the function endpoint directly.
column5: Create a NotificationConfig that specifies the Pub/Sub topic and a filter for the findings you want to export.
column6: Configure Security Command Center to write findings directly to Cloud Logging, then create a log-based alert that triggers Cloud Functions.
column8: Creating a NotificationConfig is the required first step to enable Security Command Center to publish findings to a Pub/Sub topic. The NotificationConfig defines which findings trigger notifications through a filter and specifies the destination Pub/Sub topic. Once notifications are published to Pub/Sub, Cloud Functions can be triggered by subscriptions to that topic to perform automated remediation. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-notifications

column2: You are configuring Security Command Center Premium for your organization and want to ensure that Event Threat Detection can monitor Google Workspace activity to detect threats such as external members being added to privileged Google Groups. Which configuration is required to enable this capability?
column3: Create a custom Event Threat Detection module to parse Google Workspace activity exported to Cloud Logging.
column4: Enable Data Access audit logs in all projects and configure the Google Workspace connector in Security Command Center.
column5: Activate Security Command Center at the project level and enable the Google Groups monitoring module in Event Threat Detection.
column6: Activate Security Command Center at the organization level and share Google Workspace logs with Google Cloud.
column8: Event Threat Detection can only scan Google Workspace logs when Security Command Center is activated at the organization level. Google Workspace logs track user sign-ins and actions performed in the Google Workspace Admin Console. For Event Threat Detection to monitor these logs for threats like unsafe Google Groups changes, you must share the logs with Google Cloud and have organization-level SCC activation. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-event-threat-detection-overview

column2: You have configured a VPC Service Controls perimeter protecting Cloud Storage and BigQuery. Users inside the perimeter report that they cannot access some Google Cloud APIs from VM instances within the protected VPC network, even though those APIs are not restricted by the perimeter. You want to resolve this issue while maintaining security controls. What should you do?
column3: Add the required APIs to the restricted services list in the perimeter configuration to enable VMs inside the perimeter to access them.
column4: Disable the VPC Service Controls perimeter temporarily and configure firewall rules to control API access at the network level instead of using service perimeters.
column5: Configure VPC accessible services in the perimeter to allow access to the required services by setting it to 'All restricted services' or adding specific services to the allowed list.
column6: Create an egress rule that allows VMs within the perimeter to access the required APIs outside the perimeter boundary using service account identities.
column8: VPC accessible services controls which services can be accessed from network endpoints inside the perimeter. By default, if VPC accessible services is enabled, only explicitly allowed services can be accessed from within the perimeter. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/create-service-perimeters

column2: Your security team stores threat intelligence indicators (malicious IPs, domains, file hashes) in a dedicated BigQuery table that is updated daily. You have routed Cloud Audit Logs and VPC Flow Logs to BigQuery using log sinks. You need to identify connections to known malicious IP addresses at scale with efficient query performance. Which approach should you use?
column3: Use a BigQuery SQL JOIN operation between the logs table and the threat intelligence table on the IP address field to correlate events with known IOCs.
column4: Export the threat intelligence table to a CSV file, then use Cloud Logging query language to filter logs matching the IP addresses.
column5: Configure Cloud IDS to perform real-time correlation between network traffic and the BigQuery threat intelligence table.
column6: Create a separate BigQuery view for each malicious IP address and union them together to detect matches.
column8: BigQuery's JOIN capability allows efficient correlation of large log datasets with threat intelligence tables. BigQuery uses hash-based joins to process tables across multiple workers, enabling scalable correlation of logs with IOC data. This is the most direct and efficient approach for identifying matches between logs and threat indicators. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/query-syntax

column2: Your security team needs to create custom Cloud Monitoring dashboards to visualize Security Command Center findings. A junior analyst will be responsible for building these dashboards using the Google Cloud console. What is the minimum predefined IAM role you should grant to the analyst on the project to enable them to create and modify custom dashboards?
column3: Monitoring Admin (roles/monitoring.admin)
column4: Monitoring Viewer (roles/monitoring.viewer)
column5: Security Center Admin Viewer (roles/securitycenter.adminViewer)
column6: Monitoring Editor (roles/monitoring.editor)
column8: The Monitoring Editor role provides the permissions needed to create and modify custom dashboards in Cloud Monitoring. This role includes the necessary permissions for dashboard management while following the principle of least privilege. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/charts/dashboards

column2: You are deploying a Cloud Function to automatically remediate Security Command Center findings by modifying IAM policies on affected resources. The function will be triggered by Pub/Sub messages from SCC notifications. Following the principle of least privilege, you need to configure the appropriate IAM permissions for the Cloud Function's service account. What should you do?
column3: Configure the Cloud Function to impersonate a privileged service account only when needed using short-lived credentials and the Service Account Token Creator role.
column4: Use the default Compute Engine service account with the Editor role since the function needs broad permissions to remediate various resource configurations.
column5: Grant the Security Admin role to the Cloud Function's service account at the organization level to ensure it can remediate findings across all projects.
column6: Create a dedicated service account with only the specific IAM permissions required for the remediation actions, and configure the Cloud Function to use this service account at runtime.
column8: Following the principle of least privilege, you should create a dedicated service account with only the permissions necessary for the specific remediation tasks. Cloud Functions can be configured to use a custom service account instead of the default Compute Engine service account, which typically has overly broad Editor permissions. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/functions/docs/concepts/iam

column2: Your organization wants to export Cloud Audit Logs to BigQuery for long-term security analysis. The security team requires optimized query performance with lower costs when analysts filter by date ranges. You need to configure a Cloud Logging sink to BigQuery. What configuration should you use?
column3: Configure the sink to use clustered tables in the BigQuery dataset.
column4: Configure the sink to use partitioned tables in the BigQuery dataset.
column5: Configure the sink to use date-sharded tables in the BigQuery dataset.
column6: Configure the sink to export to a linked BigQuery dataset from a log bucket.
column8: Partitioned tables allow BigQuery to scan only the partitions that match the filter and skip the remaining partitions. This process called pruning improves query performance and reduces costs when filtering by date ranges. Partitioned tables are recommended over date-sharded tables for better performance. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/bigquery

column2: Your security operations team is using Community Security Analytics (CSA) queries with Log Analytics to detect threats in your Google Cloud environment. You need to identify potential defense evasion techniques where an attacker may have modified logging configurations to hide their activities. Which log source and filter combination should you query?
column3: Enable VPC Flow Logs and query for outbound connections from Cloud Logging IP ranges to detect log exfiltration.
column4: Query Data Access audit logs and filter on protoPayload.methodName='google.logging.v2.LoggingServiceV2.ListLogEntries' to detect unauthorized log reads.
column5: Query Admin Activity audit logs and filter on protoPayload.serviceName='logging.googleapis.com' to detect changes to logging settings and log sinks.
column6: Query System Event audit logs and filter on protoPayload.serviceName='monitoring.googleapis.com' to detect alerting policy changes.
column8: Admin Activity audit logs record all configuration changes including modifications to logging infrastructure. Filtering on the logging.googleapis.com service captures attempts to disable logging, delete log sinks, or modify log bucket configurations, which are common defense evasion techniques. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit-logging

column2: Your security team is investigating a potential data exfiltration incident in Google Security Operations (SecOps). An analyst needs to determine if a suspicious domain that was recently added to threat intelligence feeds was accessed by any assets in the last 90 days. What should the analyst do?
column3: Configure a reference list with the suspicious domain and enable automated enrichment for all future events.
column4: Export all raw logs from the past 90 days to BigQuery and run a SQL query to find domain matches.
column5: Create a real-time detection rule and wait for it to trigger alerts if the domain is accessed again in the future.
column6: Run a retrohunt using a YARA-L rule that matches events containing the suspicious domain against historical data.
column8: A retrohunt enables searching historical data using existing or new detection rules. This allows analysts to search for detections throughout existing data in Google SecOps, which is ideal for investigating if assets accessed a newly identified suspicious domain within a specified time range. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/run-rule-historical-data

column2: Your organization uses Security Command Center Enterprise tier and needs to prioritize vulnerability remediation based on risk. You notice that two vulnerability findings have the same severity level, but one exposes a database containing sensitive customer data. How should you use Security Command Center to prioritize these vulnerabilities?
column3: Apply security marks to manually tag database-related vulnerability findings as higher priority.
column4: Export both findings to Google Security Operations and use YARA-L rules to assign risk scores based on affected resource types.
column5: Review the attack exposure scores assigned by the Risk Engine to compare how each vulnerability exposes your high-value resources to potential attack paths.
column6: Create custom detection rules in Event Threat Detection to increase the severity of findings related to database resources.
column8: The Risk Engine calculates attack exposure scores by simulating what attackers could do if they discovered the vulnerabilities. Findings that expose high-value resources like databases with sensitive data will have higher attack exposure scores, allowing you to prioritize remediation based on actual risk exposure rather than just severity. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/attack-exposure-learn

column2: Observability"Your organization needs to track the number of IAM policy changes across your Google Cloud environment over time to identify anomalous spikes that could indicate privilege escalation attempts. You decide to create a log-based metric to support this requirement. Which metric type and configuration should you use?
column3: Create a distribution-type log-based metric with a filter for SetIamPolicy calls and extract the number of bindings changed as the metric value.
column4: Create a distribution-type log-based metric with a filter for all IAM-related audit logs and configure histogram buckets for response time analysis.
column5: Create a counter-type log-based metric with a filter for protoPayload.methodName='SetIamPolicy' and add a label that extracts the full timestamp from each log entry.
column6: Create a counter-type log-based metric with a filter for protoPayload.methodName='SetIamPolicy' and add a label to extract the principal email from the log entries.
column8: Counter metrics count the number of log entries matching a filter, which is appropriate for tracking IAM policy change frequency. Adding a label for the principal email allows you to filter and analyze time series by user, supporting detection of anomalous activity patterns from specific principals. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics/counter-metrics

column2: Your organization wants to establish a baseline of normal administrative behavior using Cloud Identity audit logs. A security engineer asks you which specific log types in Cloud Identity should be collected to track user authentication events, administrative actions in the Google Admin Console, and group membership changes. Which three Cloud Identity audit log types should you prioritize for this baseline?
column3: OAuth Token audit logs, SAML audit logs, and Admin audit logs
column4: Data Access audit logs, Admin Activity audit logs, and Policy Denied audit logs
column5: Login audit logs, Admin audit logs, and Groups audit logs
column6: Access Transparency logs, Admin audit logs, and Login audit logs
column8: Login audit logs track user sign-in events including suspicious logins from unfamiliar IP addresses, Admin audit logs record actions performed in the Google Admin Console such as when administrators add users or change settings, and Groups audit logs track changes to group settings and group memberships which directly affect IAM permissioning in Google Cloud. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/logs-based-security-alerting-in-google-cloud

column2: Your security operations team wants to automate threat hunting when new threat intelligence is published to an external IOC feed. The system must receive IOC updates, parse them, and automatically search across historical logs in Google Security Operations (SecOps) within minutes of receiving new indicators. You need to design a solution using Google Cloud services that minimizes operational overhead and scales automatically. What should you do?
column3: Configure Event Threat Detection custom detectors in Security Command Center to monitor for IOC feed updates and automatically trigger Cloud Functions for threat hunting.
column4: Deploy a Compute Engine VM running a Python script that continuously monitors the IOC feed and pushes new indicators to the SecOps detection engine through direct database writes.
column5: Configure a Pub/Sub topic to receive IOC updates, create a Cloud Function with a Pub/Sub trigger that parses the IOC data, and calls the Google SecOps API to initiate retrohunts against the new indicators.
column6: Configure Cloud Scheduler to periodically call a Cloud Function that polls the external IOC feed, downloads all indicators, and stores them in BigQuery for manual analysis by threat hunters.
column8: This approach provides an event-driven architecture where IOC updates trigger automated processing. Cloud Functions scale automatically and Pub/Sub provides reliable message delivery for security telemetry, while the SecOps API enables programmatic retrohunt execution. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/functions/docs/calling/pubsub

column2: Your organization uses Security Command Center Premium at the organization level. A security engineer created an Event Threat Detection custom module at the organization level to detect connections to malicious IP addresses from your threat intelligence feed. A project team needs to disable this custom module for their specific project without affecting other projects. What happens when the project team disables the inherited custom module at the project level?
column3: The project team cannot disable the custom module because organization-level modules are enforced on all child resources.
column4: The custom module must be cloned to the project level before it can be modified or disabled for that project.
column5: The custom module is disabled across the entire organization because inherited modules cannot be selectively modified.
column6: The custom module is disabled only for the specific project, while remaining enabled for all other projects and folders in the organization.
column8: When you enable or disable an inherited custom module, your changes apply only to your current resource level. The original custom module residing at the parent level is not affected. This allows granular control over detection policies at different levels of the resource hierarchy. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/use-custom-modules-etd

column2: Your security team has deployed Container Threat Detection on multiple GKE clusters running container workloads. After reviewing findings, you notice that the file monitoring detectors are not generating any alerts for access to sensitive system files. What is the most likely cause and solution?
column3: The file monitoring detectors are disabled by default and must be explicitly enabled in the Container Threat Detection modules settings.
column4: The clusters are using Ubuntu-based node images, which do not support Container Threat Detection file monitoring.
column5: The GKE clusters are running GKE Sandbox, which is required for file monitoring detection capabilities to function.
column6: The containerthreatdetection API was manually disabled which prevents all Container Threat Detection functionality including file monitoring.
column8: Container Threat Detection's file monitoring detectors are disabled by default to avoid performance impacts on workloads with significant file I/O. These detectors must be manually enabled through the Modules page in Security Command Center settings. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-container-threat-detection-overview

column2: You are investigating a suspected data breach where sensitive customer data may have been exfiltrated from Cloud Storage. Your organization uses Sensitive Data Protection (Cloud DLP) to classify data and has integrated it with Security Command Center. You want to prioritize your investigation based on which Cloud Storage buckets contain the most sensitive data. What should you do?
column3: Query Security Command Center for Data sensitivity findings generated by Sensitive Data Protection data profiles to identify high-sensitivity buckets.
column4: Configure VPC Service Controls alerts to identify which buckets had perimeter violations during the investigation timeframe.
column5: Run ad-hoc DLP inspection jobs on all Cloud Storage buckets to generate new sensitivity classifications during the active incident.
column6: Export all Cloud Logging data access logs to BigQuery and manually analyze which buckets have the most read operations.
column8: Sensitive Data Protection publishes Data sensitivity findings to Security Command Center that indicate the sensitivity level of data in storage resources. These findings help prioritize investigation by showing which buckets contain PII or other sensitive elements that require immediate attention during a breach investigation. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/dlp/docs/send-profiles-to-scc

column2: You are building a SOAR playbook to automate the incident response workflow when Security Command Center detects a Discovery: Service Account Self-Investigation finding. The playbook must collect evidence, contain the threat, and preserve the audit trail. What sequence of actions should the playbook execute?
column3: First disable the service account to stop further API access, then export Cloud Audit Logs for the service account to a forensic bucket with a locked retention policy, and finally notify the incident response team with finding details.
column4: First revoke all IAM role bindings for the service account across all projects, then capture a VM snapshot of any compute instances using the account, and finally store the bindings list in a forensic bucket.
column5: First notify the incident response team with finding details, then rotate the service account key, and finally enable Cloud Audit Logging for the affected project.
column6: First export Cloud Audit Logs to a forensic bucket, then delete the service account to prevent further access, and finally create a new service account with the same name to restore services.
column8: Disabling the service account is the immediate containment action that stops all API access. Exporting Cloud Audit Logs to a forensic bucket with a locked retention policy preserves the complete audit trail in an immutable state for investigation. Notifying the team last ensures all automated preservation steps are complete before human intervention begins. This sequence prioritizes containment, then evidence preservation, then notification. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/service-accounts-disable-enable and https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/bucket-lock

column2: Your organization wants to centrally collect audit logs from all projects within a folder hierarchy and route them to a Cloud Storage bucket for long-term retention. You need to ensure that logs continue to be stored locally in each project's _Default bucket while also being sent to the central Cloud Storage bucket. Which sink configuration should you use?
column3: Create an intercepting aggregated sink at the folder level with the --include-children flag to route logs to the Cloud Storage bucket.
column4: Create individual project-level sinks in each project pointing to the central Cloud Storage bucket with identical filters.
column5: Create a non-intercepting aggregated sink at the folder level with the --include-children flag to route logs to the Cloud Storage bucket.
column6: Create a sink at the organization level without the --include-children flag and configure each project to inherit the sink configuration.
column8: A non-intercepting aggregated sink does not affect how log entries are routed to other sinks, including the _Default sink in each project. This ensures logs are both routed to the central Cloud Storage bucket and continue to be stored in each project's local log buckets. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/aggregated_sinks

column2: You are configuring an Event Threat Detection custom module to detect connections to known malicious domains discovered by your security research team. You have created the JSON template with the domain list and custom remediation guidance. Before deploying to production, you want to verify the module's configuration and understand the operational constraints. Which two statements about Event Threat Detection custom modules are correct?
column3: Custom modules have a size limit of 10 MB per module and can process logs from any external source configured in Cloud Logging.
column4: Custom modules run alongside built-in detectors in real-time mode and have a default quota limit of 200 modules per organization.
column5: Custom modules can override the behavior of built-in detectors and disable default threat intelligence sources to reduce false positives.
column6: Security Command Center automatically provides remediation recommendations for all custom module findings based on the threat category.
column8: Event Threat Detection custom modules run alongside built-in detectors, enabled modules run in real-time mode that triggers scans whenever new logs are created, and the default quota limit for custom modules is 200. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/custom-modules-etd-overview

column2: Your security operations team needs to use Sensitive Data Protection data profiles to enrich asset context in Google Security Operations (SecOps). You want to ensure that when a security alert involves a BigQuery table, analysts can quickly understand the data sensitivity classification. What is the recommended approach to achieve this integration?
column3: Use the DLP API's content.inspect method within a SOAR playbook to scan data assets in real-time whenever a security alert is triggered.
column4: Enable the integration between Sensitive Data Protection discovery service and Security Command Center, then configure SCC findings to flow into Google SecOps for correlation with alerts.
column5: Export DLP data profiles to a separate BigQuery dataset and configure Google SecOps to query this dataset for real-time data sensitivity lookups during alert processing.
column6: Configure Pub/Sub notifications from DLP discovery scans to trigger Cloud Functions that update custom labels on BigQuery tables for SecOps entity enrichment.
column8: Sensitive Data Protection has direct integration with Security Command Center, where data sensitivity and data risk findings are surfaced. Security Command Center Enterprise integrates with Google SecOps, allowing these DLP findings to be correlated with security alerts, enriching the asset context for analysts during investigations. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/dlp-sensitive-data-intelligence-now-available-in-scc

column2: Your organization needs to track the count of failed authentication attempts across your Google Cloud environment for security monitoring purposes. You want to visualize trends over time in Cloud Monitoring dashboards and create alerting policies when the count exceeds a threshold. You need to determine the appropriate log-based metric type. Which metric type should you use?
column3: Distribution-type log-based metric with a filter matching failed authentication log entries.
column4: Boolean-type log-based metric with a filter matching failed authentication log entries.
column5: Counter-type log-based metric with a filter matching failed authentication log entries.
column6: System-defined log-based metric for authentication failures with custom labels added.
column8: Counter metrics count the number of log entries that match a specified filter within a specific period. They are designed for tracking how many times a value or string appears in logs, making them ideal for counting security events like failed authentication attempts. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics/counter-metrics

column2: A developer needs to run Terraform code to provision Google Cloud resources in a production project. The developer's user account does not have direct permissions to create resources. Your security team requires that no service account keys be used and all actions are traceable to the individual developer. You need to configure the least privileged access. What should you do?
column3: Grant the developer the Service Account User role on a dedicated service account and configure Terraform to authenticate using the attached service account.
column4: Grant the developer the Editor role at the project level to provide the necessary permissions for provisioning resources directly.
column5: Create a service account key for the dedicated service account and distribute it securely to the developer using Secret Manager.
column6: Grant the developer the Service Account Token Creator role on a dedicated service account, and configure Terraform to use impersonation with the --impersonate-service-account flag.
column8: Granting Service Account Token Creator allows the developer to impersonate the service account without creating service account keys. All actions are logged with the developer's identity in Cloud Audit Logs through the serviceAccountDelegationInfo section. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/service-account-impersonation

column2: Your organization is using Google Security Operations (SecOps) with Applied Threat Intelligence (ATI). You notice that your analysts are overwhelmed with IOC match alerts. You want to configure detection rules that prioritize alerts based on indicators that Mandiant has observed in active breach investigations, where the Google Threat Intelligence verdict is malicious and severity is high. Which ATI priority model should you enable?
column3: Enable the Active Breach priority model in the ATI Curated Prioritization rule pack.
column4: Enable the Inbound IP address authentication model in the ATI Curated Prioritization rule pack.
column5: Enable the Medium priority model in the ATI Curated Prioritization rule pack.
column6: Enable the High priority model in the ATI Curated Prioritization rule pack.
column8: The Active Breach model specifically prioritizes indicators that Mandiant observed in active or past compromises where the GTI Verdict is Malicious and GTI Severity is High. This model uses features including GTI Verdict, GTI Severity, Active IR, Prevalence, and Attribution to identify the highest priority threats. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/ati-prioritization

column2: Detection engineering"Your organization recently received a new threat intelligence report containing IOCs for a previously unknown campaign. You have already created a YARA-L detection rule for these IOCs and want to search for any historical matches in your Google Security Operations (SecOps) data from the past 30 days. What should you do?
column3: Convert the YARA-L rule to a UDM search query and manually search for matching events using the Search feature with a 30-day time range selected.
column4: Export the past 30 days of UDM events to BigQuery and run the YARA-L rule as a scheduled query against the exported dataset for historical analysis.
column5: Run a retrohunt on the YARA-L rule with a time range covering the past 30 days to search for detections throughout existing data in Google SecOps.
column6: Enable the rule in live mode and wait for the detection engine to automatically backfill detections from the past 30 days during its scheduled processing cycles.
column8: Retrohunt in Google SecOps allows you to run a detection rule against historical data to find matches that occurred before the rule was created. This is the intended method for searching existing data with new detection logic. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/run-rule-historical-data

column2: Your organization requires monitoring of a security service API endpoint that is only accessible from within your private VPC network. The endpoint responds to HTTPS requests on port 443. You need to configure uptime monitoring to detect availability issues. What should you do?
column3: Create a synthetic monitor using a Cloud Run function deployed in your VPC with Serverless VPC Access to reach the internal endpoint.
column4: Create a private uptime check using Service Directory with a servicedirectory_service monitored resource type targeting the internal IP address.
column5: Configure a public uptime check with HTTPS protocol and add a VPN connection from Google's uptime check servers to your VPC.
column6: Create a public uptime check using the Internal IP resource type and configure firewall rules to allow traffic from uptime check servers.
column8: Private uptime checks use Service Directory to monitor internal IP addresses within VPC networks. The servicedirectory_service resource type is required for private uptime checks, and it allows monitoring of resources that are not publicly accessible. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/uptime-checks/private-checks

column2: Platform operations"You are configuring Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) for multiple web applications in your organization. Different applications require different access levels - some need only IP-based restrictions while others require device posture verification. When multiple access levels are applied to a single IAP-secured resource, how does IAP evaluate them for a user request?
column3: When multiple access levels are applied to a resource, IAP evaluates them using AND logic - the user must satisfy all applied access levels to gain access.
column4: IAP prioritizes access levels by creation date and evaluates only the most recently created access level, ignoring older ones.
column5: IAP evaluates access levels in alphabetical order and grants access based on the first matching access level encountered.
column6: When multiple access levels are applied to a resource, IAP evaluates them using OR logic - the user is granted access if they satisfy at least one of the applied access levels.
column8: When you apply multiple access levels to a single IAP-secured resource, IAP uses logical OR evaluation. This means users are granted access when they meet the conditions specified in at least one of the selected access levels. This behavior allows administrators to define different acceptable contexts for access. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/beyondcorp-enterprise/docs/access-levels

column2: Your organization receives hundreds of Security Command Center findings daily, but only critical and high-severity findings require immediate automated notification. You need to configure a notification workflow that sends only these findings to a Slack channel using Cloud Functions. What is the most efficient approach?
column3: Create a NotificationConfig that exports all findings to Pub/Sub, and implement severity filtering logic within the Cloud Function to process only critical and high findings.
column4: Create a NotificationConfig with a filter expression that specifies severity = 'CRITICAL' OR severity = 'HIGH' and state = 'ACTIVE' to export only matching findings to a Pub/Sub topic that triggers the Cloud Function.
column5: Configure Security Command Center to send findings directly to the Slack API endpoint using the built-in webhook integration without requiring Cloud Functions.
column6: Create two separate NotificationConfigs with different filters for CRITICAL and HIGH severity findings, each publishing to separate Pub/Sub topics with dedicated Cloud Functions.
column8: NotificationConfig supports filter expressions that limit which findings are published to the Pub/Sub topic. By filtering at the source, only relevant findings trigger the Cloud Function, reducing unnecessary function invocations and processing overhead. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-api-filter-notifications

column2: Your security team is using Security Command Center Enterprise to manage posture findings. They want to integrate with ServiceNow for ticket management so that remediation tasks are tracked in their existing workflow system. After integrating ServiceNow, how does Security Command Center Enterprise handle the relationship between cases and tickets?
column3: Security Command Center requires manual ticket creation through playbook actions after each case is generated by the connector.
column4: Security Command Center creates one ticket for each case and automatically synchronizes case content and updates with the corresponding ticket.
column5: Security Command Center exports finding data to ServiceNow on a scheduled batch basis without real-time synchronization.
column6: Security Command Center creates one ticket for each individual finding, with separate tickets linked to a parent case ticket.
column8: When you integrate with a ticketing system, Security Command Center creates a new ticket every time it creates a new case for findings. A single case can contain multiple findings, but one ticket is created per case. Security Command Center automatically updates the related ticket whenever a case is updated, synchronizing case content and information with the corresponding ticket. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/integrate-ticketing-systems

column2: Your security team has developed a common workflow for communicating with clients during incident investigations. This workflow is used across multiple playbooks for different alert types. You want to implement this workflow efficiently so that any updates to the workflow automatically apply to all playbooks that use it. What should you do?
column3: Duplicate the communication workflow steps in each playbook and use version control to track changes across all playbooks.
column4: Create a separate standalone playbook for client communication and manually trigger it from each parent playbook using a webhook action.
column5: Create a reusable playbook block with input parameters and insert it into parent playbooks that require the client communication workflow.
column6: Create a custom integration that implements the communication workflow and call it as an action from each playbook.
column8: Playbook blocks are reusable mini-playbooks that let you implement common workflows across multiple playbooks. Any edit or change to a block automatically affects all playbooks that incorporate it, and input parameters make blocks flexible and adaptable. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/working-with-playbook-blocks

column2: Your organization needs to retrieve asset metadata that includes relationships between Compute Engine instances and their associated disks using Cloud Asset Inventory. The organization currently has only Security Command Center Standard tier. What is required to enable this capability?
column3: Upgrade to Security Command Center Premium or Enterprise tier to enable the RELATIONSHIP content type in Cloud Asset Inventory.
column4: Use the gcloud scc assets list command to retrieve instance and disk relationship metadata from Security Command Center directly.
column5: Configure a Cloud Asset Inventory feed with the RESOURCE content type and export to BigQuery to analyze disk relationships.
column6: Enable the Cloud Asset Inventory API and use the IAM_POLICY content type to view disk associations for each VM instance.
column8: Relationship types in Cloud Asset Inventory require access to Security Command Center Premium or Enterprise tier, or Gemini Cloud Assist. Without this tier, you cannot retrieve asset relationship metadata such as COMPUTE_INSTANCE_USE_DISK. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/asset-inventory/docs/relationship-types

column2: Your organization activated Security Command Center Premium at the organization level and wants to monitor Google Workspace for potential account compromise and unauthorized access. What is required to enable Event Threat Detection to scan Google Workspace logs?
column3: Create a custom module that uses the Unexpected OAuth Token Access template to detect suspicious Google Workspace authentication events.
column4: Enable the Google Workspace Event Threat Detection module in Security Command Center settings and provide your Google Workspace admin credentials.
column5: Activate Security Command Center Premium at the project level for each project that needs Google Workspace threat detection capabilities.
column6: Share your Google Workspace logs with Google Cloud by configuring Google Workspace to export logs to Cloud Logging at the organization level.
column8: Event Threat Detection can monitor Google Workspace logging streams only when Security Command Center is activated at the organization level AND Google Workspace logs are shared with Google Cloud. Google Workspace logs track user sign-ins and Admin Console actions. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-event-threat-detection-overview

column2: Your security team notices that some log entries exported via a Cloud Logging sink are missing from the BigQuery destination tables. Upon investigation, you find an 'export_errors' table in the dataset. You need to identify the cause of this issue. What is the most likely reason?
column3: A schema mismatch occurred when log entries had different field types than the existing table schema.
column4: The sink filter was modified to exclude certain log types after the initial configuration.
column5: The BigQuery streaming insert quota was exceeded for the destination table.
column6: The destination dataset region does not match the Cloud Logging sink region.
column8: When BigQuery identifies a schema mismatch, it creates an error table (export_errors for partitioned tables or export_errors_YYYYMMDD for date-sharded tables) to store the error information. Schema mismatches occur when a later log entry changes the field type for an existing field, such as when a field is an integer in one entry but a string in another. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/bigquery

column2: You are configuring uptime checks for multiple security services across your organization. You need to grant a team member permission to create and modify uptime checks and alerting policies using the Google Cloud console. Which IAM role should you assign?
column3: roles/monitoring.viewer
column4: roles/monitoring.admin
column5: roles/monitoring.notificationChannelEditor
column6: roles/monitoring.editor
column8: The Monitoring Editor role grants permissions to create, update, and delete uptime checks and alerting policies. This role provides the necessary access to configure monitoring resources through the Google Cloud console without granting broader administrative permissions. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/alerts/using-alerting-ui

column2: During incident response, your team needs to isolate a group of GKE nodes that have been compromised by malware. The nodes are running critical workloads and you cannot immediately terminate them. You want to use IAM-governed tags to apply containment firewall rules without impacting legitimate workloads on other nodes. What is the correct sequence of actions?
column3: Update the GKE node pool configuration to add custom network tags, then create a hierarchical firewall policy rule that blocks traffic to tagged instances.
column4: Create a VPC Service Controls perimeter around the compromised nodes' project and configure ingress/egress rules to deny all traffic.
column5: Create a network firewall policy with deny rules targeting a specific secure tag value, bind the secure tag to the compromised nodes, then associate the policy with the VPC network.
column6: Add a network tag to the compromised nodes, create a VPC firewall deny rule targeting that network tag, then remove compute.instances.setTags permission from node pool service accounts.
column8: IAM-governed secure tags provide controlled access through IAM permissions, preventing unauthorized users from removing containment tags from VMs. Network firewall policies with secure tags can be quickly applied to specific nodes without affecting other workloads. Binding tags to nodes applies immediately and triggers the firewall policy enforcement. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/tags-firewalls-overview

column2: Your organization has recently activated Security Command Center Enterprise and wants to automate case creation from Security Health Analytics misconfiguration findings. You need to configure the ingestion connector so that posture findings are automatically converted into cases for your security analysts to triage. Which connector should you configure in the Security Operations console to enable automated case creation from posture findings?
column3: Security Command Center API Polling Connector
column4: SCC Enterprise – Threat Detection Connector
column5: Google Chronicle – Chronicle Alerts Connector
column6: SCC Enterprise – Urgent Posture Findings Connector
column8: The SCC Enterprise – Urgent Posture Findings Connector is specifically designed to ingest Security Command Center posture findings, analyze them, and automatically group them into new or existing cases based on finding type. This connector is the primary mechanism for automated case creation from Security Health Analytics and other posture-related findings. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/integrate-ticketing-systems

column2: Threat hunting"You are configuring the integration between Security Command Center (SCC) and Google Security Operations (Chronicle) for a threat hunting use case. Your goal is to correlate SCC toxic combination findings with threat intelligence to identify scenarios where exploitable attack paths align with known threat actor activity. Which approach best accomplishes this objective?
column3: Ingest SCC toxic combination findings into Chronicle, then create composite detection rules that correlate toxic combination data with Applied Threat Intelligence IOC matches on the same resources.
column4: Export SCC toxic combination findings to BigQuery and join them with Chronicle IOC match data exported to the same BigQuery dataset.
column5: Configure SCC's Risk Engine to incorporate Google Threat Intelligence feeds directly into attack path simulations and adjust toxic combination scores accordingly.
column6: Enable Event Threat Detection to monitor for threat activity on resources identified in toxic combination findings and configure alerts based on severity overlap.
column8: Chronicle's composite detection lets you interconnect rules so that the output of one rule acts as input for another. By correlating SCC toxic combination findings (which identify attack paths to high-value resources) with ATI IOC matches, you can identify scenarios where known threat actor activity aligns with exploitable paths in your environment. This provides proactive threat hunting by combining posture risk with active threat intelligence. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/composite-rules and https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/applied-threat-intel-overview

column2: Your SOC uses Google Security Operations (SecOps) SOAR for incident response. You need to ensure that all case activity, including automated playbook actions, manual analyst activities, and collaboration messages, is captured in a single searchable location for audit and compliance purposes. Where should analysts access this information?
column3: The Cloud Audit Logs in the Google Cloud console, which captures all API calls and administrative actions across the SOAR platform.
column4: The SOAR Dashboards page, which aggregates all case metrics and analyst performance data in real-time visualizations.
column5: The SIEM Search page, which indexes all case-related activity alongside security event data for correlation.
column6: The Case Wall within each case, which automatically documents all playbook action results, manual actions, and collaboration content.
column8: The Case Wall is the auto-documenting feature that captures all SOC activity including automated actions, manual activities, chats, tasks, and uploaded files in a single, searchable, and auditable repository within each case. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security/products/security-operations

column2: Your security operations team is using Google Security Operations (SecOps) and wants to identify any assets that have communicated with IP addresses matching known threat indicators from Mandiant threat intelligence. Your organization has Applied Threat Intelligence (ATI) enabled with an Enterprise Plus license. How should you view and prioritize these matches?
column3: Use UDM Search to query for all network connections and manually cross-reference results with exported Mandiant threat intelligence feeds.
column4: Navigate to the IoC Matches page and filter by Sources to show only Mandiant indicators, then prioritize based on GCTI Priority labels such as Active IR or High.
column5: Create a custom YARA-L rule to detect connections to Mandiant threat indicators and enable alerting on all matches regardless of confidence score.
column6: Configure a SOAR playbook to export all network logs daily and send them to Mandiant's API for external threat matching analysis.
column8: The IoC Matches page displays all indicators of compromise matched in your data against threat intelligence feeds. With ATI enabled, you can filter by Sources to view Mandiant IoCs and use GCTI Priority labels to prioritize investigation of the most critical matches. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/ati-view-ioc-page

column2: Your security team receives too many alerts from the Applied Threat Intelligence (ATI) curated detection rules in Google Security Operations (SecOps). Many alerts are from Medium priority indicators that are not immediately actionable. You need to reduce alert volume while maintaining coverage for critical threats. What should you do?
column3: Configure rule exclusions for all IP addresses that match RFC 1918 internal ranges to automatically exclude internal traffic from ATI matching.
column4: Increase the GTI score threshold to 95 in the ATI configuration settings to filter out low-confidence indicators before they generate alerts.
column5: Keep the ATI Medium priority rule packs in non-alerting mode while keeping High and Active Breach rule packs with alerting enabled.
column6: Disable all ATI curated detection rule packs and create custom YARA-L rules that only match on indicators with GTI verdict of Malicious and High severity.
column8: Google recommends keeping ATI medium rule packs in non-alerting mode due to the potential volume of Medium priority indicators. High and Active Breach priority rule packs should remain in alerting mode to maintain coverage for critical threats. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/ati-prioritization

column2: You are investigating a potential breach in Google Security Operations (SecOps) and discovered a suspicious domain in your network traffic. You want to leverage VirusTotal to understand the relationships between this domain and potentially malicious infrastructure, including visualizing connections to related IPs, file hashes, and other domains. What should you do?
column3: Use the Enrich Entities action in a SOAR playbook to automatically generate a relationship graph for the domain.
column4: Navigate to the IOC matches page and use the Associations tab to view the VirusTotal relationship graph for the domain.
column5: Query the entity graph in Google SecOps using UDM search to retrieve all related indicators connected to the domain.
column6: Open the Domain view in Google SecOps, navigate to the Graph tab, and launch VirusTotal Graph using your VirusTotal Enterprise credentials.
column8: VirusTotal Graph within Google SecOps analyzes the relationship between files, URLs, domains, IP addresses, and other items. It helps illustrate the interconnections between potentially malicious domains and assets within your enterprise. To use VirusTotal Graph, you must have a VirusTotal Enterprise account and can launch it from the Graph tab in Domain view, IP address view, or Hash view. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/investigation/view-virustotal-information

column2: Data management"You have configured a Cloud Logging sink to export security logs to a BigQuery dataset. After several months of operation, your security team reports that some recent log entries are appearing in a table named export_errors instead of the expected log table. You need to identify the root cause and prevent this issue from recurring. What is the most likely cause of this issue?
column3: The BigQuery dataset has exceeded its storage quota, causing new log entries to be redirected to an overflow error table for later processing.
column4: A log entry contained a field with a data type that conflicts with an existing column in the BigQuery table schema, causing a schema mismatch error.
column5: The log entries have timestamps that are too old for real-time streaming insertion, causing BigQuery to reject them and store them in an error table.
column6: The sink's service account permissions have expired, causing authentication failures that result in log entries being written to an error table.
column8: When BigQuery identifies a schema mismatch, such as a field type change for an existing field, it creates an export_errors table to store the problematic log entries. The first log entry determines the schema, and subsequent entries with conflicting field types cause mismatches. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/bigquery

column2: A security analyst reviews Web Security Scanner findings in Security Command Center and discovers multiple XSS (cross-site scripting) vulnerabilities in a production web application. The analyst needs to verify the findings before escalating to the development team. How should the analyst verify the XSS vulnerability findings?
column3: Check the finding's JSON definition for the externalUri field and manually inspect the page source code.
column4: Follow the Reproduction URL provided in the finding details, which produces an empty popup in the browser when the vulnerability is confirmed.
column5: Run a manual penetration test using external tools like OWASP ZAP to independently verify the vulnerability exists.
column6: Review the Cloud Audit Logs for the affected application to confirm exploitation attempts have occurred.
column8: Web Security Scanner provides a Reproduction URL for XSS findings that, when followed, produces an empty popup in the browser to confirm the scan successfully injected benign code into a script. This is the recommended verification method documented by Google. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-remediate-web-security-scanner-findings

column2: Your organization uses Security Command Center Premium tier at the organization level. You need to implement real-time alerting so your security operations team receives immediate email notifications when Event Threat Detection identifies high or critical severity threats. What should you do?
column3: Create a BigQuery dataset for continuous export of ETD findings, then use Data Studio to create an email alert dashboard that sends notifications hourly.
column4: Configure Event Threat Detection to send email notifications directly to your security team by updating the service settings in the Security Command Center console.
column5: Configure a continuous export to Pub/Sub with a filter for high and critical severity ETD findings, then deploy a Cloud Run function to send email notifications via SendGrid or a similar service.
column6: Enable Cloud Logging for Event Threat Detection and configure a log-based alert to send notifications when high or critical findings appear.
column8: Continuous exports to Pub/Sub provide near real-time notification of findings that match specified filters. By combining this with a Cloud Run function, you can transform findings into email notifications. This architecture enables automated alerting workflows for security operations. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-enable-real-time-notifications

column2: You are configuring VPC Service Controls for a Google Cloud environment. Your organization requires that VMs inside the perimeter can only access the specific Google Cloud services that are protected by the perimeter and no other services. How should you configure this restriction?
column3: Enable VPC accessible services for the perimeter and set it to 'All restricted services' to allow only the services protected in the perimeter.
column4: Configure the restricted.googleapis.com VIP as the only DNS endpoint for Google APIs from within the VPC network.
column5: Configure firewall rules on the VPC network to block outbound traffic to Google API IP ranges except for the protected services.
column6: Add egress rules that explicitly deny access to all services not listed in the restricted services configuration.
column8: The VPC accessible services feature limits the set of services accessible from network endpoints inside your service perimeter. Setting it to 'All restricted services' ensures that VMs inside can only access the services you have protected in the perimeter, preventing access to other Google Cloud services. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/create-service-perimeters

column2: You are building a Google Security Operations (SecOps) SOAR playbook for handling phishing incidents that requires manager approval before quarantining an endpoint. The IT manager who must approve the action does not have access to the Google SecOps platform. You need to configure the playbook to enable this external approval workflow. What should you do?
column3: Create a custom integration that polls an external ticketing system for approval status before executing the quarantine action.
column4: Configure the quarantine action as Manual, enable the Approval link toggle, and add a preceding Send Email action that includes the Approve and Decline link placeholders.
column5: Configure the quarantine action as Automatic and create a separate manual approval step that assigns the action to a SOC role for proxy approval.
column6: Configure the quarantine action as Automatic and add a Time to respond deadline that auto-approves if no response is received.
column8: Approval links allow you to send manual actions waiting for user input (pending actions) to users outside of the platform. By enabling the Approval link toggle and including the generated placeholders in an email, external users can approve or decline actions without platform access. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/assign-approval-links-in-actions

column2: Your organization needs to implement Event Threat Detection custom modules to detect connections to a large set of malicious IP addresses from your threat intelligence platform. The threat feed contains over 100,000 IP addresses and is updated weekly. What constraint should you consider when planning this implementation?
column3: Event Threat Detection custom modules can only process static configurations and do not support automated updates from external threat feeds.
column4: Each Event Threat Detection custom module has a size limit of 6 MB, so you may need to split the IP addresses across multiple custom modules.
column5: Custom modules only support CIDR notation and cannot accept individual IP addresses, so all 100,000 IPs must be aggregated into CIDR blocks.
column6: Event Threat Detection custom modules have a hard limit of 1,000 indicators per module that cannot be increased through quota requests.
column8: Each Event Threat Detection custom module has a maximum size limit of 6 MB. With a large number of IP addresses, the JSON template may exceed this limit, requiring the IOCs to be distributed across multiple custom modules. Additionally, there is a default quota of 200 custom modules per organization. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/custom-modules-etd-overview

column2: Your security team has detected a potentially compromised container image running in your GKE production cluster. The image was deployed using Binary Authorization with a 'Disallow all images' default policy. You need to deploy a critical security patch immediately while ensuring the incident is properly logged for forensic analysis. What should you do?
column3: Add the patched container image to the admissionWhitelistPatterns in the Binary Authorization policy and deploy immediately.
column4: Create a new attestor and manually sign the patched image, then wait for the attestation to propagate before deploying the container.
column5: Disable Binary Authorization enforcement on the cluster, deploy the patched container, then re-enable enforcement after deployment completes.
column6: Add the 'image-policy.k8s.io/break-glass: true' label to the Pod specification and deploy the patched container, then query Cloud Audit Logs for breakglass events.
column8: The breakglass label allows you to override Binary Authorization policy enforcement in emergency situations. When images are deployed with breakglass, Binary Authorization logs breakglass events in Cloud Audit Logs, providing a documented audit trail for incident response and forensic analysis. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/using-breakglass

column2: Your organization has enabled Security Command Center Premium tier at the organization level. The security team reports that the OPEN_FIREWALL detector is generating many findings for firewall rules that are intentionally configured to allow traffic on specific ports for internal testing purposes. You want to suppress these findings for the testing environment without disabling the detector globally. What should you do?
column3: Configure Event Threat Detection custom modules to filter out OPEN_FIREWALL findings from the testing project.
column4: Disable the OPEN_FIREWALL detector module in Security Health Analytics settings for the entire organization.
column5: Create a dynamic mute rule with a filter that matches findings from the testing project and the OPEN_FIREWALL category.
column6: Add a security mark 'allow_open_firewall:true' to each testing project to exclude them from the detection policy.
column8: Dynamic mute rules allow you to automatically suppress findings based on specified criteria such as project and finding category without disabling the detector entirely. Dynamic mute rules are recommended over static rules as they offer more flexibility and can apply to both existing and future findings. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-mute-findings

column2: Your organization needs to implement a centralized security log analysis solution where logs from all projects across your Google Cloud organization are correlated with an external threat intelligence feed containing known malicious IP addresses. You want to route Cloud Audit Logs to BigQuery and perform JOIN operations against a threat intelligence table to detect potential threats. What should you do first?
column3: Configure a Log Analytics linked dataset and route logs to a read-only BigQuery dataset for threat correlation.
column4: Create an organization-level aggregated sink that routes audit logs to a BigQuery dataset in a dedicated security project.
column5: Create project-level log sinks in each project that route logs directly to the threat intelligence system for analysis.
column6: Enable Data Access audit logs and configure a Pub/Sub topic as the sink destination for real-time threat matching.
column8: Aggregated sinks at the organization level can collect and route log entries from all projects in the resource hierarchy to a centralized BigQuery dataset, enabling consistent analysis and JOIN operations with threat intelligence data. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/aggregated_sinks

column2: Your security operations team uses Google SecOps with Applied Threat Intelligence enabled. Analysts report that they are receiving numerous IOC match alerts from the ATI Fusion Feed, but many are low-confidence indicators that consume investigation time. You need to optimize the alerting configuration to focus analyst attention on the most actionable threats. What should you do?
column3: Keep ATI Medium Priority rule packs in non-alerting mode and enable alerting only for Active Breach Priority and High Priority rule packs, which filter IOCs based on GTI verdict and severity.
column4: Disable the Applied Threat Intelligence feature and create custom YARA-L rules that only match IOCs you manually import from trusted intelligence sources.
column5: Configure rule exclusions for all ATI rule packs to filter out IOCs that have been seen more than 10 times in the past week to reduce noise from common indicators.
column6: Increase the default IC-Score threshold for all ATI rule packs from 80 to 95 to reduce the number of IOCs that trigger alerts.
column8: Google recommends keeping ATI Medium Priority rule packs in non-alerting mode due to the potential volume of Medium priority indicators. Active Breach and High Priority rule packs use the GTI verdict (Malicious with High severity) and additional features like Active IR status to prioritize the most actionable IOCs. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/ati-prioritization

column2: Your security team has received threat intelligence from a trusted third-party vendor containing a list of IP addresses associated with known command-and-control servers. You need to configure Event Threat Detection in Security Command Center to generate findings when any VM in your environment connects to these IP addresses. Which approach should you use?
column3: Export the IP addresses to Google Threat Intelligence (GTI) and configure Event Threat Detection to use GTI for matching.
column4: Create a Configurable Bad IP custom module with the IP addresses from the threat intelligence feed and set the appropriate severity level.
column5: Modify the built-in Malware: Bad IP detector to include the third-party IP addresses in its detection logic.
column6: Create a Security Health Analytics custom module with IP address validation rules that trigger alerts on connection events.
column8: The Configurable Bad IP custom module template is specifically designed to detect connections to user-supplied IP addresses. When logs indicate a connection to any of the supplied IP addresses, a finding is generated and written to Security Command Center. This allows you to extend Event Threat Detection with your own custom threat intelligence. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/custom-modules-etd-overview

column2: Security Command Center Enterprise detected a Malware: Bad IP finding indicating that a Compute Engine VM communicated with a known command and control IP address. You want to use this finding to perform proactive threat hunting and determine if other resources in your environment have communicated with similar malicious infrastructure. What should you do?
column3: Use the Flow Analyzer URL from the SCC finding to investigate VPC Flow Logs for the specific VM that triggered the finding.
column4: Create an Event Threat Detection custom module using the Configurable Bad IP template with the malicious IP address and enable it to detect future communications.
column5: Ingest the SCC finding into Google SecOps, extract the malicious IP from the finding, and create a YARA-L rule to search for other events involving that IP or related IOCs across all ingested telemetry.
column6: Export the finding to Cloud Logging and configure a log-based alert to notify the security team when new findings reference the same IP address.
column8: SCC findings can be ingested into Google SecOps and analyzed alongside other security telemetry.
