Cloud Asset Inventory is the recommended replacement, and it 'discovers assets automatically, so you do not need to enable or otherwise configure discovery.' Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-api-configure-asset-discovery

column2: You are designing a Looker Studio dashboard architecture to visualize Security Command Center findings exported to BigQuery. The dashboard will be used by multiple teams, including the SOC team and compliance auditors. You want to ensure that compliance auditors only see findings related to their specific projects while the SOC team sees all findings. How should you configure the data access?
column3: Create separate reusable data sources with SQL queries filtered by project, and share each data source with the appropriate team.
column4: Create one report for the SOC team and share it broadly, then rely on BigQuery row-level access policies to restrict auditor visibility.
column5: Configure filter by email address in a single data source to dynamically show project-specific findings based on the viewer's email.
column6: Use Looker Studio Pro team workspaces to manage access, with separate workspaces for SOC and compliance teams.
column8: Creating separate reusable data sources with project-filtered SQL queries allows you to control data access at the data source level. The SOC team uses an unfiltered data source while compliance auditors use a filtered one. Reusable data sources provide better governance since access can be managed independently of reports. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/looker/docs/studio/data-governance-in-looker-studio-an-overview

column2: Your organization activated Security Command Center Premium and wants to analyze all cloud assets across the entire organization. The security operations team notices that the Assets page in Security Command Center displays asset information. Where does Security Command Center obtain this asset inventory data?
column3: Security Command Center requires you to enable asset discovery in Organization Settings before assets are populated on the Assets page.
column4: Security Command Center imports asset data from Cloud Logging by analyzing resource creation events in Cloud Audit Logs.
column5: Security Command Center maintains its own independent asset discovery service that scans all Google Cloud resources in the organization.
column6: Security Command Center reads asset data directly from Cloud Asset Inventory, which automatically discovers and catalogs assets across the organization.
column8: As of the current implementation, Security Command Center's Assets page obtains its asset inventory data from Cloud Asset Inventory. Cloud Asset Inventory automatically discovers assets without requiring separate configuration in Security Command Center. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/work-with-resources-in-the-console

column2: A security analyst reports that requests from specific corporate office IP addresses are being denied access to Cloud Storage buckets protected by a VPC Service Controls perimeter. The requests originate from users who should have access based on their corporate location. You need to allow access from these IP addresses while maintaining perimeter security. What should you do?
column3: Create an egress rule that allows the service perimeter to send responses to the corporate IP address ranges.
column4: Create an access level in Access Context Manager with the corporate office public IP address ranges, and add the access level to the service perimeter configuration.
column5: Add the corporate office VPC network to the perimeter as a member network to allow traffic from the corporate network endpoints.
column6: Configure an ingress rule on the perimeter that specifies the corporate IP address ranges in the ingressFrom sources field and allows access to all resources.
column8: Access levels enable you to define conditions based on client attributes such as IP address ranges. When you add an access level to a perimeter, requests that meet the access level conditions can access protected resources from outside the perimeter without requiring additional ingress rules. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/use-access-levels

column2: Your security team has received a list of 500 malicious IP addresses from a threat intelligence feed. You need to search for connections to these IP addresses in Cloud Logging data that spans the past 90 days. The data resides in a log bucket that has been upgraded to Log Analytics. You want to implement a scalable and cost-effective solution for this threat hunting activity. What should you do?
column3: Configure Cloud Logging sinks to stream all logs to Pub/Sub and build a real-time matching application to check against the IOC list.
column4: Create a linked BigQuery dataset from the log bucket, upload the IOC list as a BigQuery table, and use a SQL JOIN query to correlate log entries with the malicious IP addresses.
column5: Export all logs from the past 90 days to Cloud Storage, download the files locally, and use a Python script to search for the malicious IP addresses.
column6: Use the Logs Explorer to manually search for each IP address by entering individual filter queries for all 500 IP addresses sequentially.
column8: Creating a linked BigQuery dataset enables you to join log data with external datasets like IOC lists. This approach allows scalable SQL-based correlation, supports large IOC lists efficiently, and enables repeated queries without additional data movement costs. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/analyze/query-linked-dataset

column2: Your organization has implemented Google Security Operations (SecOps) SOAR and needs to standardize the case escalation workflow. When high-priority cases are detected, you want to automatically notify the assigned SOC Manager, update the case stage to Assessment, and create a task for a Tier 2 analyst to review. You want to implement this using the most efficient approach. What should you do?
column3: Configure a Quick Actions widget in the case view to allow analysts to manually execute the escalation workflow with a single click.
column4: Create a playbook block that includes the Change Case Stage action, Assign Case action, and Email > Send Email action, then incorporate this block into existing playbooks that handle high-priority cases.
column5: Create a separate standalone playbook with a priority trigger that fires on high-priority cases to execute the Change Case Stage, Assign Case, and Send Email actions sequentially.
column6: Write a custom Python integration in the IDE that uses the SOAR API to update case stages, send notifications, and create tasks programmatically.
column8: Playbook blocks are reusable mini-playbooks that let you implement common workflows across multiple playbooks. Any edit to a block automatically affects all playbooks that incorporate it, making this the most efficient and maintainable approach for standardizing escalation workflows. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/working-with-playbook-blocks

column2: You are implementing SLO monitoring for a custom security scanning service that doesn't correspond to an automatically detected microservice in Cloud Monitoring. The service uses custom metrics to track scanning success rates. What should you do to enable SLO monitoring for this security service?
column3: Use the Monitoring API to create metric-based alerting policies instead of SLOs since custom services cannot have SLOs defined.
column4: Create a custom service in Cloud Monitoring and then define SLOs using custom metrics in the SLI configuration.
column5: Configure the security scanning service as a Cloud Service Mesh service to enable automatic SLI detection and SLO creation.
column6: Export the custom metrics to an external monitoring system that natively supports SLO monitoring for custom applications.
column8: When no existing service type accommodates an application, you can define a custom service. Custom services allow you to arbitrarily group SLOs together and create SLOs on business metrics that don't correspond to an existing microservice. You can then specify custom metrics as the SLI for your SLO. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring/ui/define-svc

column2: Your security operations team needs to receive immediate notifications when any user accesses a service account key from the Google Cloud console. You want to implement a solution that notifies the team each time this specific security event occurs in your audit logs. Which alerting approach should you use?
column3: Configure a SQL-based alerting policy in Log Analytics to query for the service account key access event.
column4: Create a user-defined counter log-based metric with an alerting policy that monitors when the count exceeds zero.
column5: Create a system-defined log-based metric alerting policy that monitors audit log access patterns.
column6: Create a log-based alerting policy from Logs Explorer using a filter that matches the service account key access event.
column8: Log-based alerting policies are designed for security-related events where you need to be notified when a specific message occurs in a log entry. As stated in the documentation, they are 'useful for catching security-related events in log entries, like...a human user accesses the security key of a service account.' Log-based alerting policies trigger on individual log entries matching your query. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/alerting/log-based-alerts

column2: Detection engineering"Your organization is using Security Command Center Premium and needs to detect when Compute Engine instances are created in regions that violate your organization's data residency policy. The built-in Security Health Analytics detectors do not cover this specific requirement. You want to implement a detection mechanism that runs automatically when new instances are created. What should you do?
column3: Create a Security Health Analytics custom module that uses CEL expressions to check if compute.googleapis.com/Instance resources are created in non-approved regions.
column4: Create a Cloud Asset Inventory feed with a Pub/Sub notification and Cloud Functions to generate custom findings when instances are created in non-approved regions.
column5: Configure an Event Threat Detection custom module using the Configurable allowed Compute Engine region template to monitor for instance creation in restricted regions.
column6: Enable the built-in COMPUTE_REGION_VIOLATION detector in Security Health Analytics and configure it with your list of approved regions.
column8: Security Health Analytics custom modules support real-time scans that are triggered whenever an asset's configuration changes, including when new resources are created. Custom modules use YAML definitions with CEL expressions to specify the detection logic. You can specify one to five resource types to scan and define predicates to check resource properties like region. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/custom-modules-sha-overview

column2: You are configuring Google Security Operations (SecOps) to ingest Cloud Audit Logs and Access Transparency logs for security analysis. You want to correlate customer administrative actions with any Google personnel access to establish a complete privileged access baseline. What is the key difference between these two log sources?
column3: Cloud Audit Logs record actions by your organization's members while Access Transparency logs record actions taken by Google personnel.
column4: Access Transparency logs are enabled by default for all projects while Cloud Audit Logs require explicit configuration.
column5: Cloud Audit Logs are stored in the _Default bucket while Access Transparency logs require custom log sink configuration.
column6: Cloud Audit Logs capture only read operations while Access Transparency logs capture both read and write operations by any user.
column8: Cloud Audit Logs record the actions that members of your Google Cloud organization have taken in your Google Cloud resources, whereas Access Transparency logs record the actions taken by Google personnel. When used together, they provide audit logging on both customer actions and Google administrative access to Customer Data. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/assured-workloads/access-transparency/docs/overview

column2: You need to monitor a security scanning service and determine whether it meets its service-level objectives. The service must respond to scanning requests within 200ms for 95% of requests over a calendar month. You need to select the appropriate SLI configuration in Cloud Monitoring. Which approach should you use?
column3: Configure a windows-based SLI using availability as the metric type and filter for responses completed within 200ms.
column4: Configure a request-based SLI using latency as the metric type and set the threshold to 200ms to define what constitutes a good request.
column5: Configure an availability SLI with the SLO goal set to 200ms and the compliance period set to one calendar month.
column6: Create a custom metric that records latency values and use a distribution-cut indicator with a percentile threshold of 95%.
column8: Request-based SLIs measure individual requests against a goodness criterion. For latency-based SLOs, you configure a threshold (200ms) where requests below that latency are counted as good, and the SLO target (95%) specifies what percentage must be good. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring/ui/create-slo

column2: Your organization experienced a security incident where an attacker used compromised service account credentials to exfiltrate data from Cloud Storage buckets. You want to prevent similar incidents by ensuring that even with valid credentials, data cannot be copied to external destinations. Which approach should you implement?
column3: Configure IAM Conditions on Cloud Storage buckets to restrict access based on source IP addresses of authorized networks.
column4: Create VPC firewall rules that deny egress traffic from all VMs to the Cloud Storage service IP ranges.
column5: Configure VPC Service Controls with an enforced perimeter that restricts Cloud Storage API access and blocks data copying to resources outside the perimeter.
column6: Implement VPC Service Controls in dry run mode to log all data access operations and block suspicious transfers automatically.
column8: VPC Service Controls prevent data exfiltration by restricting service operations such as copying data to resources outside the perimeter, even when using valid credentials. An enforced perimeter actively blocks requests that violate the policy, protecting against both stolen credentials and malicious insiders. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/overview

column2: You are performing threat hunting on GKE clusters and want to investigate Container Threat Detection findings. You need to understand how Container Threat Detection collects runtime telemetry from your GKE nodes. Which architecture component is responsible for collecting and passing container event information to the detector service?
column3: A GKE-managed control plane component that intercepts all container runtime calls through the Kubernetes API server.
column4: A sidecar container automatically injected into each pod by the Container Threat Detection admission controller.
column5: A central logging agent deployed as a Kubernetes Deployment that polls container logs from all nodes periodically.
column6: A user mode DaemonSet deployed in the kube-system namespace with the label k8s-app=container-watcher.
column8: Container Threat Detection passes event information through a user mode DaemonSet to a detector service for analysis. This DaemonSet runs in the kube-system namespace and can be identified by the label k8s-app=container-watcher. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-use-container-threat-detection

column2: Your incident response team has identified a sophisticated attack where compromised VMs are communicating with command-and-control servers using encrypted connections on standard HTTPS port 443. You need to implement network-level containment that blocks these specific malicious destinations while allowing legitimate business traffic. What approach should you use?
column3: Enable VPC Service Controls dry-run mode to monitor API calls and configure egress policies to block unauthorized external data transfers.
column4: Deploy Cloud IDS sensors and configure them to automatically block detected malicious traffic by integrating with VPC firewall rules.
column5: Configure VPC firewall rules with destination IP addresses of the command-and-control servers and deny all egress traffic on port 443 to those addresses.
column6: Create a global network firewall policy with egress deny rules using FQDN objects that specify the known command-and-control server domain names, and assign appropriate priority.
column8: Network firewall policies support FQDN (Fully Qualified Domain Name) objects that can be used as destinations in egress rules. This allows you to block traffic to specific malicious domains on port 443 while allowing legitimate HTTPS traffic to other destinations. The policy is evaluated based on DNS resolution of the specified FQDNs. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewall-policies-rule-details

column2: During an active security incident, your incident response team needs to rapidly contain multiple compromised VMs across different projects within a Shared VPC environment. You need to implement firewall rules that can be centrally managed and applied consistently across all affected VMs. Which firewall configuration approach should the playbook specify?
column3: Create a global network firewall policy with high-priority deny rules and associate it with the Shared VPC network to block traffic for VMs with specific secure tags.
column4: Create individual VPC firewall rules in each service project targeting VMs by their internal IP addresses to block all suspicious traffic.
column5: Deploy hierarchical firewall policies at the organization level with network tags to immediately isolate the compromised VMs across all projects.
column6: Configure VPC Service Controls perimeters around each compromised project to prevent network communication between the affected VMs.
column8: Global network firewall policies are defined at the project level and can be associated with multiple VPC networks, enabling centralized management across a Shared VPC environment. Secure tags provide IAM-governed targeting that cannot be modified by users without appropriate permissions. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/network-firewall-policies

column2: Your SOC team wants to track incident response efficiency metrics such as mean time to resolve (MTTR) and cases closed by analyst over time. Google Security Operations (SecOps) data is already exported to BigQuery. You need to create a long-term reporting solution that executives can access without requiring BigQuery expertise. What should you do?
column3: Query the BigQuery tables directly in the Google Cloud console and export results as CSV files to share with executives on a weekly basis for trend analysis.
column4: Connect Looker Studio to the BigQuery dataset containing case data using the BigQuery connector and create an interactive dashboard with calculated fields for MTTR and analyst performance metrics.
column5: Create custom YARA-L rules in Google SecOps to calculate MTTR and display results in the SIEM dashboard for executive review.
column6: Export case data from BigQuery to Google Sheets on a scheduled basis and create pivot tables for executives to analyze incident response trends and analyst performance.
column8: Looker Studio provides a self-service BI platform that can connect directly to BigQuery using the native connector. Executives can view interactive dashboards without needing SQL expertise, and calculated fields can derive metrics like MTTR from raw case timestamps. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/visualize-looker-studio

column2: You have created a Cloud Monitoring dashboard with charts displaying log-based metrics derived from Security Command Center findings. You need to configure an alerting policy that notifies the security team when high-severity findings exceed a threshold. However, the security team reports that alerting is inconsistent. What should you check first to resolve this issue?
column3: Change the alerting policy from metric-based to log-based alerting to receive notifications for individual log entries instead.
column4: Configure the notification channel to use multiple delivery methods to ensure the security team receives alerts reliably.
column5: Increase the alert threshold value to reduce the number of false positive notifications being generated.
column6: Verify the Rolling window setting is at least 10 minutes for log-based metrics and configure how the policy handles missing data.
column8: Log-based metric time series can have data gaps and values of zero. For alerting policies monitoring log-based metrics, Google recommends setting the rolling window to at least 10 minutes and configuring how the policy handles missing data to avoid inconsistent alerting behavior. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics#missing-data

column2: You have activated Security Command Center Premium tier and enabled Event Threat Detection. Your security operations team reports that they are not seeing any Malware: Bad Domain findings even though you suspect malicious DNS activity in your environment. What is the most likely cause of this issue?
column3: The Malware: Bad Domain detector must be manually enabled in the Event Threat Detection modules settings.
column4: Event Threat Detection findings are only visible in Cloud Logging, not in the Security Command Center console.
column5: Cloud DNS logging is not enabled, which is required for Event Threat Detection to detect malware using domain resolution.
column6: Event Threat Detection requires the Enterprise tier of Security Command Center to generate Malware: Bad Domain findings.
column8: Event Threat Detection can detect malware using domain resolution only when Cloud DNS logging is enabled. Some logs that Event Threat Detection scans are turned off by default, and Cloud DNS logs are essential for detecting Malware: Bad Domain findings. For network detection of malware through domain resolution, Cloud DNS logs are typically sufficient for most users. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-event-threat-detection-overview

column2: You have configured a user-defined log-based counter metric to track authentication failures in your Cloud Logging environment. Security analysts report that the alerting policy monitoring this metric is generating false positive notifications during periods of low activity. You want to reduce false notifications while maintaining detection accuracy. What should you do?
column3: Increase the rolling window value in the alerting policy condition to at least 10 minutes to ensure multiple matching log entries are counted before triggering an alert.
column4: Modify the counter metric filter to use stricter matching criteria and reduce the number of labels to limit time series cardinality.
column5: Configure the alerting policy to use a log-based alert instead of a metric-based alert to eliminate timing delays in metric aggregation.
column6: Enable backfill for the log-based metric to populate historical data and establish a consistent baseline for anomaly detection.
column8: Log-based metric data can have gaps that result in false notifications during periods of low activity. Google documentation recommends increasing the rolling window value to reduce false positives, specifically stating that 'the value should be large enough to make sure that multiple log entries that match your filter are counted.' A minimum of 10 minutes is recommended for alignment period. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics/charts-and-alerts

column2: Your organization has enabled Security Command Center Premium tier and wants to deploy Container Threat Detection to monitor GKE clusters. Several of your clusters are running workloads in GKE Sandbox to provide additional isolation for untrusted code. You need to ensure Container Threat Detection can protect your containerized workloads. What should you do?
column3: Configure Container Threat Detection to monitor only the control plane logs using Event Threat Detection while GKE Sandbox handles runtime protection.
column4: Enable Container Threat Detection and configure it to use user-space monitoring mode that is compatible with GKE Sandbox workloads.
column5: Create separate node pools for GKE Sandbox workloads and Container Threat Detection to ensure they operate on different nodes.
column6: Disable GKE Sandbox on the clusters where you want to deploy Container Threat Detection since they are not compatible.
column8: Container Threat Detection is not compatible with GKE Sandbox. The documentation explicitly states that GKE Sandbox must be disabled on clusters where you want Container Threat Detection deployed. This is because Container Threat Detection's kernel-level instrumentation conflicts with gVisor's sandboxing mechanism. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-use-container-threat-detection

column2: Your organization uses Security Command Center Premium and Google Security Operations (SecOps). Event Threat Detection has identified a suspicious outbound connection to a known malicious IP address. You need to determine if the same IP address has been observed elsewhere in your environment over the past 30 days. What is the most efficient approach?
column3: Use Cloud Logging's Logs Explorer to search for the IP address across all log entries from the past 30 days using a filter query.
column4: Ingest SCC findings into Google SecOps, then use the IOC matches page to view all events associated with the malicious IP address across your security telemetry.
column5: Create a continuous export from SCC to Pub/Sub and configure a Cloud Function to search for the IP address in Cloud Armor logs.
column6: Export the SCC finding to BigQuery and run a SQL query to search for the IP address across all Cloud Audit Logs from the past 30 days.
column8: Google SecOps automatically correlates ingested IoCs against your security telemetry and displays all matches on the IOC matches page. This provides visibility into all instances where the malicious IP appeared in your environment, including historical data up to your retention period. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/investigation/alerts-iocs

column2: A compliance team at your organization requires visibility into when Google personnel access your organization's customer data stored in Google Cloud. They need to establish a baseline of Google administrative access patterns and alert when access exceeds a threshold. Which combination of Google Cloud features should you use to meet this requirement?
column3: Configure Cloud Identity Login Audit logs, export to Google SecOps, and create detection rules for anomalous access
column4: Enable Access Transparency logs, configure a logs-based metric in Cloud Monitoring, and set up an alerting policy with defined thresholds
column5: Enable Data Access audit logs for all services, route to a Cloud Storage bucket, and use Cloud Functions to analyze access frequency
column6: Enable Cloud Audit Logs Admin Activity logging, create a BigQuery export sink, and schedule daily queries to analyze access patterns
column8: Access Transparency logs record actions taken by Google personnel when accessing customer data. You can monitor these logs using Cloud Monitoring API, create logs-based metrics to capture access patterns, and configure alerting policies that trigger when access exceeds specified thresholds. This approach enables both baseline establishment and anomaly detection. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/assured-workloads/access-transparency/docs/reading-logs

column2: Your organization uses Security Command Center Enterprise with Security Health Analytics enabled. A security analyst notices that when a finding is remediated, the corresponding case remains open for several hours before closing. The analyst wants to understand when the case will automatically close. What triggers the automatic closure of a case created from Security Health Analytics findings?
column3: The case closes immediately when the resource configuration is corrected in Google Cloud, as Security Health Analytics monitors changes in real-time.
column4: The analyst must manually close the case after verifying remediation by running the Close Case action in the Security Operations console.
column5: When all findings in the case are either set to INACTIVE state by Security Health Analytics after detecting remediation or are muted, the case is automatically closed.
column6: The case closes after 24 hours based on the Sync SCC Data job schedule configured in the SOAR Settings.
column8: Security Command Center automatically closes a case when all findings it contains are either inactive or muted. Security Health Analytics sets a finding state to INACTIVE when it detects that the underlying misconfiguration has been remediated during its next scan cycle. If you mute all findings in a case, the case is also closed automatically. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-use-security-health-analytics and https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/mute-findings-in-cases

column2: Your security team has created an isolated forensic project in Google Cloud for incident investigations. You need to configure IAM access so that only the incident response team can upload forensic evidence to the storage bucket, while ensuring no one can delete or modify existing evidence. Which IAM configuration should you implement?
column3: Grant the incident response team the Storage Legacy Bucket Writer role on the forensic bucket and configure an IAM Deny policy to block object deletion.
column4: Grant the incident response team the Storage Object Admin role (roles/storage.objectAdmin) on the forensic bucket and enable Object Versioning to track all changes.
column5: Grant the incident response team the Storage Admin role (roles/storage.admin) on the project and use Cloud Audit Logs to monitor for unauthorized deletions.
column6: Grant the incident response team the Storage Object Creator role (roles/storage.objectCreator) on the forensic bucket and configure a locked retention policy on the bucket to prevent deletion.
column8: The Storage Object Creator role allows uploading new objects but does not grant permissions to read, modify, or delete existing objects. Combined with a locked retention policy, this ensures that evidence can be collected but cannot be tampered with or removed until the retention period expires. This implements the principle of least privilege while maintaining evidence integrity. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/iam-roles and https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/bucket-lock

column2: Your organization has standardized a communication workflow for escalating high-severity incidents to stakeholders. This workflow involves sending approval requests via email, waiting for customer confirmation, and updating case stages based on the response. Multiple investigation playbooks across different environments need to use this identical escalation process. You want to implement this workflow efficiently while minimizing maintenance overhead. What should you do?
column3: Create a playbook block with configurable input parameters for communication type and method, then insert this block into each parent playbook that requires the escalation workflow.
column4: Copy and paste the escalation action sequence into each playbook manually, using placeholders to maintain consistency across different environments and alert types.
column5: Create a separate escalation playbook and configure alert triggers to attach it as an additional playbook whenever high-severity alerts are generated.
column6: Build a dedicated connector that triggers an external escalation service and integrate it as an action step within each playbook requiring the workflow.
column8: Playbook blocks are reusable mini-playbooks that can be inserted into multiple parent playbooks. Blocks support input parameters to customize their behavior and can return output values to parent playbooks. Any edit to a block automatically affects all playbooks that incorporate it, reducing maintenance overhead. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/working-with-playbook-blocks

column2: Your security team observes that Security Health Analytics generates a large number of findings for resources in a development project that are intentionally configured with relaxed security settings for testing purposes. You want to suppress these findings for the development project while ensuring that new and existing findings in production projects remain visible. You also want the flexibility to easily reverse this suppression if the development project moves to production. What should you do?
column3: Add security marks to resources in the development project to exclude them from Security Health Analytics detectors.
column4: Create a dynamic mute rule with a filter that matches findings from the development project and configure it without an expiration date.
column5: Disable Security Health Analytics for the development project using Security Command Center Services settings.
column6: Create a static mute rule with a filter that matches findings from the development project.
column8: Dynamic mute rules can mute both existing and future findings based on filter criteria. When configured without an expiration date, they act indefinitely but can be easily deleted to reverse the suppression. Unlike static mute rules, dynamic rules automatically unmute findings when the rule is removed. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-mute-findings

column2: Your organization needs to detect when cloud resources connect to IP addresses from your organization's private threat intelligence feed. The threat intelligence team regularly updates this feed with new indicators. You have Security Command Center Premium tier activated at the organization level. What is the most appropriate approach to implement this detection capability?
column3: Create an Event Threat Detection custom module using the Configurable Bad IP template with your organization's maintained IP address list.
column4: Export VPC Flow Logs to Google SecOps and create YARA-L rules that match against a reference list containing your threat intelligence IP addresses.
column5: Configure Security Health Analytics custom detectors to scan network configurations for connections to the malicious IP addresses.
column6: Configure the built-in Malware: Bad IP detector in Event Threat Detection to include your organization's custom IP address list.
column8: Event Threat Detection custom modules allow you to define detection parameters using your own threat intelligence. The Configurable Bad IP custom module template scans VPC Flow Logs for connections to IP addresses you maintain, runs alongside built-in detectors in real-time, and generates findings when matches are detected. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/custom-modules-etd-overview

column2: Your security team needs to detect lateral movement activity where a user authenticates to multiple distinct hosts within a short time frame. You want to create a YARA-L rule in Google Security Operations (SecOps) that triggers only when the same user connects to more than three unique hostnames within a 15-minute window. Which YARA-L rule structure should you use?
column3: Use a multi-event rule with a match section that groups by $user over 15m and a condition section that checks #hostname > 3.
column4: Use a single-event rule with the over keyword in the events section to specify the 15-minute time window for user authentication events.
column5: Create a rule with a condition section that uses count($hostname) > 3 without a match section to detect multiple host connections.
column6: Implement a composite rule that chains multiple single-event authentication rules and aggregates results using detection-only mode.
column8: Multi-event YARA-L rules use the match section to group events by a common field (user) over a time window (15m), and the condition section can use the '#' operator to count distinct values of the hostname variable, triggering when more than three unique hosts are detected. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/yara-l-2-0-overview

column2: You are configuring VPC Service Controls for a Shared VPC environment with a host project and multiple service projects. After enabling the perimeter, service projects are unable to access protected APIs. What is the most likely cause and solution?
column3: The service projects need egress rules configured to allow API access through the host project's network configuration.
column4: VPC accessible services are not enabled for the perimeter. Enable VPC accessible services and add all restricted services to the allowed list.
column5: The Shared VPC host project is not included in the same service perimeter as the service projects. Add the host project to the perimeter.
column6: The perimeter needs to be recreated at the folder level using a scoped policy that includes both the host and service projects.
column8: When using Shared VPC, you must include the host project in a service perimeter along with any projects that belong to the Shared VPC. Network endpoints belonging to service projects appear to be outside the perimeter if only service projects are included, since subnets are associated with the host project. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/service-perimeters

column2: Your organization uses Sensitive Data Protection discovery to profile BigQuery tables. A table profile shows a 'High' data risk level even though the sensitivity level is only 'Moderate'. You need to understand why the data risk is elevated. What is the most likely explanation?
column3: The profiling job did not complete successfully, causing incomplete risk calculation and default elevated risk assignment.
column4: The inspection template used for profiling included too many infoTypes, causing false positives that elevated the risk score.
column5: The table contains moderate-sensitivity data but has no access controls to restrict data exposure, resulting in elevated data risk.
column6: The table contains free-form text columns which automatically elevate data risk regardless of detected infoTypes.
column8: Data risk level considers both the sensitivity level of the data and the presence of access controls. A table with moderate-sensitivity data that is widely accessible or lacks access controls will receive a higher data risk level than its sensitivity alone would indicate. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/sensitivity-risk-calculation

column2: You are configuring Container Threat Detection for your organization's GKE clusters. Your security team requires detection of modifications to critical system files such as /etc/shadow and /etc/pam.d on container hosts. After enabling Container Threat Detection, you notice that these file monitoring detections are not being generated. What is the most likely cause?
column3: Container Threat Detection requires the Premium tier of Security Command Center which has not been activated.
column4: The Container Threat Detection DaemonSet has not been deployed on the GKE cluster nodes.
column5: The file monitoring detectors are disabled by default to avoid performance degradation on workloads with significant file I/O.
column6: The GKE clusters are using GKE Sandbox which is incompatible with file-level monitoring.
column8: Container Threat Detection includes file monitoring detectors that monitor for access or modification to critical system files. These detectors are disabled by default because workloads with significant file I/O, such as CI/CD systems, could potentially suffer performance degradation when these detectors are enabled. You must explicitly enable them. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-container-threat-detection-overview

column2: Your organization is using Security Command Center Enterprise tier and you notice that some vulnerability findings have higher severity levels than their default category severity. You need to understand why certain findings are being escalated in severity. What is causing this behavior?
column3: Security Health Analytics custom modules have been configured with override rules that increase severity based on resource labels.
column4: Risk Engine has calculated high attack exposure scores for these findings, which automatically increases the severity level when they expose designated high-value resources.
column5: Event Threat Detection has correlated these vulnerabilities with active threat indicators, automatically elevating their severity classification.
column6: The findings are associated with toxic combinations that have been identified by the posture management service, triggering automatic severity escalation.
column8: In the Enterprise tier, finding severity levels can dynamically change based on attack exposure scores calculated by Risk Engine. When attack path simulations determine that a finding exposes high-value resources, the severity level increases accordingly to reflect the actual risk, and can decrease if the exposure score decreases. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/finding-severity-classifications

column2: Incident response"Your security team is preparing to implement VPC Service Controls as part of your incident response containment strategy. Before enforcing a new service perimeter that would isolate a critical production project during incidents, you want to validate that the containment configuration will not disrupt legitimate business operations. What should you do?
column3: Enable VPC Service Controls audit logging on the production environment and retrospectively analyze access patterns from the past 30 days to predict containment impact.
column4: Create a service perimeter in dry-run mode with the planned containment configuration, trigger a test workload, and analyze the violation logs to identify potential disruptions before enforcement.
column5: Deploy the enforced service perimeter during a maintenance window and immediately roll back if production issues are detected within a monitoring period.
column6: Create an identical test service perimeter in enforced mode in a non-production project and simulate the containment workflow with synthetic traffic.
column8: Dry-run mode allows testing of VPC Service Controls configurations without blocking access. Requests that would violate the perimeter are logged but not denied, allowing you to identify and resolve potential issues before moving to enforced mode during an actual incident. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/dry-run-mode

column2: Your organization uses Google Security Operations (SecOps) and exports security data to BigQuery. You need to implement automated weekly reports that calculate the total number of incidents by severity and the average case resolution time for the previous week. The reports should be stored in a dedicated BigQuery table for historical tracking. What should you do?
column3: Configure the Google SecOps BigQuery export to automatically generate summary metrics tables alongside the raw event data export.
column4: Create a BigQuery scheduled query that runs weekly, calculates incident metrics from the exported SecOps data, and writes results to a dedicated reporting table with date partitioning.
column5: Use Looker Studio scheduled email delivery to send weekly dashboard snapshots, then manually save the results to BigQuery for historical records.
column6: Develop a Cloud Function that queries BigQuery daily and aggregates the results into a Google Sheet, then configure Looker Studio to read from the Sheet.
column8: BigQuery scheduled queries allow you to automate recurring SQL queries that calculate metrics and store results in destination tables. Using date partitioning enables efficient historical tracking and querying of weekly metrics over time. Scheduled queries can run automatically on a weekly schedule without manual intervention. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/scheduling-queries

column2: Your organization has deployed Google Security Operations (SecOps) and needs to perform post-incident analysis on historical detection data to identify trends in rule effectiveness over time. You want to analyze which detection rules generate the most false positives versus true positives. Which BigQuery table should you query?
column3: udm_events_aggregates table, which stores aggregated data summarized by hour of normalized events.
column4: ingestion_metrics table, which stores statistics related to ingestion and normalization of data from various sources.
column5: rule_detections table, which stores detections returned by rules run in Google SecOps including rule metadata and detection timestamps.
column6: ioc_matches table, which stores all indicator of compromise matches found against UDM events.
column8: The rule_detections table specifically stores detections returned by rules run in Google SecOps. This table contains the rule identifiers, detection timestamps, and related event data needed to analyze rule effectiveness and trends over time. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/reports/overview-chronicle-bigquery

column2: You are configuring Container Threat Detection for your GKE environment. A security architect asks you to explain how Container Threat Detection collects runtime telemetry from containers. Which statement accurately describes the Container Threat Detection architecture?
column3: Container Threat Detection uses a sidecar container injected into each pod that streams events directly to Security Command Center.
column4: Container Threat Detection uses a kernel module installed on each node that intercepts system calls and sends them to Cloud Logging.
column5: Container Threat Detection uses an external agent deployed in a dedicated monitoring namespace that polls container metrics via the Kubernetes API.
column6: Container Threat Detection uses a user mode DaemonSet that passes event information and container details to a detector service for analysis.
column8: Container Threat Detection passes event information and information that identifies the container through a user mode DaemonSet to a detector service for analysis. Event collection is configured automatically when Container Threat Detection is enabled. The watcher DaemonSet passes container information in a best effort manner. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-container-threat-detection-overview

column2: Your security operations team has created a Looker Studio dashboard displaying Security Command Center findings from BigQuery. Multiple analysts need to collaborate on developing and maintaining the dashboard, and you want to ensure that if an analyst leaves the organization, the dashboard remains accessible. You are using Looker Studio Pro. What should you do?
column3: Create a team workspace and move the dashboard and data sources into the workspace, then add analysts as Contributors.
column4: Create a Google Group containing all analysts and share the dashboard with the group as Editors.
column5: Share the dashboard with individual analysts using the Share button and grant Editor permissions to each user.
column6: Export the dashboard configuration to a JSON file and store it in a shared Cloud Storage bucket for version control.
column8: Team workspaces in Looker Studio Pro enable team collaboration in a shared space. When you create content in or move content into a team workspace, all members have access to the assets. If a member leaves the organization, remaining members can still access any assets that the former member added. The organization owns content created in Looker Studio Pro team workspaces, eliminating orphaned report issues. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/looker/docs/studio/about-team-workspaces

column2: You are configuring Google Security Operations (SecOps) to automatically enrich security incidents with threat intelligence from VirusTotal. Your organization requires automated enrichment for file analysis, URL analysis, and the ability to search historical VirusTotal data for previously flagged malicious indicators. Which integration capability supports all these requirements?
column3: Configure the standard VirusTotal integration with a free API key and enable automated enrichment for all entity types.
column4: Configure Applied Threat Intelligence to ingest VirusTotal crowdsourced indicators and enable automated file submissions.
column5: Configure the VirusTotal v3 integration with Premium API access to enable file analysis, URL analysis, and retrohunting capabilities.
column6: Enable native VirusTotal file metadata enrichment in Google SecOps without any additional API configuration.
column8: The VirusTotal v3 integration supports file analysis, URL analysis, and retrohunting capabilities to search historical VirusTotal data for files, URLs, IPs, or domains that were previously flagged as malicious. This integration requires VirusTotal Premium API. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/marketplace-integrations/virustotal-v3

column2: Your organization's Security Operations team has detected a suspicious IAM role grant that may indicate a privilege escalation attempt. A user was granted the roles/owner role on a production project at an unusual time. You need to investigate the incident by identifying who performed this action and what specific changes were made. Which Cloud Audit Logs query approach should you use?
column3: Query Admin Activity audit logs filtering on protoPayload.methodName containing 'SetIamPolicy' and examine the protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail and protoPayload.serviceData.policyDelta.bindingDeltas fields.
column4: Query System Event audit logs filtering on resource.type equal to 'project' and examine the protoPayload.authorizationInfo field for permission grants.
column5: Query Data Access audit logs filtering on protoPayload.methodName containing 'SetIamPolicy' and examine the protoPayload.request.policy field for role binding information.
column6: Query Admin Activity audit logs filtering on protoPayload.serviceName equal to 'iam.googleapis.com' and examine the protoPayload.response.bindings field for current policy state.
column8: Admin Activity audit logs capture SetIamPolicy calls which modify IAM permissions, and the authenticationInfo.principalEmail field identifies who performed the action. The policyDelta.bindingDeltas field shows the specific role additions or removals, including the role granted and the member affected. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit/understanding-audit-logs

column2: You are configuring the SCC Enterprise - Urgent Posture Findings Connector for your organization's Security Command Center Enterprise deployment. Your team wants to ensure that findings are assigned to the correct resource owners for remediation. You need to configure the connector to determine ownership properly. What is the correct order of precedence that the connector uses to identify resource owners?
column3: Cloud tags inherited from the finding resource, then Essential Contacts, then the Fallback Owner parameter value.
column4: Essential Contacts, then cloud tags inherited from the finding resource, then the Fallback Owner parameter value.
column5: Fallback Owner parameter value, then Essential Contacts, then cloud tags inherited from the resource.
column6: IAM policy bindings on the resource, then project-level Essential Contacts, then organization-level Essential Contacts.
column8: The connector first analyzes findings for cloud tag values inherited from the finding resource. If no cloud tags are present, it attempts to define the resource owner using Essential Contacts. If neither source provides ownership information, the connector uses the Fallback Owner parameter value configured in the connector settings. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/determine-ownership-posture-findings

column2: You have enabled Container Threat Detection in Security Command Center Premium tier for your organization. After deploying a new GKE cluster, you notice that Container Threat Detection is not generating findings for that cluster. The cluster is running a supported version of GKE with Container-Optimized OS nodes. What is the most likely cause of this issue?
column3: The Container Threat Detection service agent has been deleted from the project, preventing findings from being generated.
column4: The cluster nodes do not have sufficient memory resources to run the Container Threat Detection DaemonSet, causing the pods to fail.
column5: Container Threat Detection is not enabled by default for new clusters and must be manually enabled in the Security Command Center settings after cluster creation.
column6: The cluster is in a private VPC without proper network configuration to communicate with Google APIs and services required by Container Threat Detection.
column8: For Container Threat Detection to work, if the cluster is in a VPC, its network must meet routing, firewall, and DNS requirements to communicate with Google APIs and services. Private clusters require Private Google Access or Private Service Connect configuration. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-use-container-threat-detection

column2: You are configuring Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) to protect a web application. Your security policy requires that users must come from the corporate network (10.0.0.0/8) AND use an encrypted device to access the application. You have created an access level named 'corp_secure' in Access Context Manager that includes both IP subnet and device encryption requirements. What must you verify about the access level configuration?
column3: Verify that Endpoint Verification is installed and the access level is configured with ALLOW_INVALID_OR_MISSING mode to permit gradual rollout.
column4: Verify that the access level is defined at the organization level access policy and both conditions are configured within the same access level with AND semantics.
column5: Verify that the access level is applied directly to the backend service using gcloud compute backend-services update command.
column6: Verify that two separate access levels are created at the project level and both are selected in the IAP binding.
column8: Access levels used with IAP must be set in the organizational access policy (scoped policies are not supported by IAP). For multiple conditions that must all be met, they should be configured within the same access level where conditions within an access level are combined using AND semantics by default. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/iap/docs/cloud-iap-context-aware-access-howto

column2: Your organization has an Organization Policy constraint enforced at the organization level that denies specific Compute Engine regions. A project team has submitted a request to be exempted from this policy. You need to configure the project to allow the denied regions while maintaining the organization-level restrictions for other projects. Which action should you take at the project level?
column3: Grant the project team the Organization Policy Administrator role to modify the constraint themselves.
column4: Create a project-level organization policy that sets inheritFromParent to FALSE and allows the needed regions.
column5: Delete the organization-level policy and recreate it with an exception for the specific project.
column6: Create a project-level organization policy that sets inheritFromParent to TRUE and adds the needed regions to the allowed list.
column8: Setting inheritFromParent to FALSE prevents the policy from inheriting the parent's settings, allowing you to define a completely different policy at the project level. This effectively exempts the project from the organization-level restriction while maintaining restrictions for other projects. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/understanding-hierarchy

column2: Your organization uses Google Security Operations (SecOps) with Applied Threat Intelligence enabled. You want to understand why a specific IOC was assigned its current priority level. The indicator is a domain that was flagged with 'High' priority. Which information sources does the ATI prioritization model consider when assigning the High priority level to domain indicators?
column3: Number of VirusTotal engine detections, domain age, whois registration data, and historical DNS records.
column4: GTI Verdict, GTI Severity, Prevalence, and Attribution to threat actors or malware tracked by Mandiant.
column5: GTI Verdict, GTI Severity, Active IR status, Prevalence, and network direction indicators.
column6: IC-Score threshold, malware family classification, geographic origin, and MITRE ATT&CK technique mappings.
column8: The High model prioritizes indicators that weren't observed in Mandiant investigations but were identified by Google Threat Intelligence as being associated with threat actors or malware. The relevant features used by this model include GTI Verdict, GTI Severity, Prevalence, and Attribution. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/ati-prioritization

column2: Your organization has deployed Google Security Operations (SecOps) and wants to identify users who have significantly deviated from their historical behavior patterns. You need to configure the Risk Analytics dashboard to detect both rapid behavioral changes and slow, persistent attacks. Which configuration approach should you use?
column3: Set the risk calculation window to 24 hours only and manually adjust entity risk scores using multiplication factors for long-term pattern detection.
column4: Configure a single 7-day risk calculation window and rely solely on base entity risk scores to identify all types of behavioral deviations.
column5: Create custom YARA-L rules to replace the Risk Analytics dashboard functionality for user behavior baseline monitoring.
column6: Use both 24-hour and 7-day risk calculation windows and compare normalized entity risk trends between windows to identify different attack patterns.
column8: The Risk Analytics dashboard supports both 24-hour and 7-day risk calculation windows. According to Google documentation, brute force attacks are more apparent when setting the Risk Calculation Window to 24 hours, while longer time frames help spot long-term attacks. Comparing normalized entity risk trends across both windows provides comprehensive behavioral baseline deviation detection. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/risk-analytics-dashboard

column2: You are creating a Cloud Monitoring dashboard to visualize security posture data from Security Command Center. You want to display the distribution of findings across different compliance frameworks such as CIS and NIST. Which widget configuration provides the most effective visualization?
column3: Configure a line chart widget with multiple data series, one per compliance framework, to show how each framework's finding counts change over time.
column4: Add a pie chart widget that uses a log-based metric with labels for compliance framework, allowing you to see the proportional distribution of findings per framework.
column5: Use a gauge widget to display the total finding count with color thresholds based on compliance risk levels for overall posture assessment.
column6: Create a table widget that lists each compliance framework with its associated finding count and severity breakdown for detailed analysis.
column8: Pie charts in Cloud Monitoring can display the proportional breakdown of metric values. By creating a log-based metric with labels extracted from the compliance framework field in SCC findings, you can visualize how findings are distributed across different compliance standards. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/charts

column2: Observability"Your organization has set up a continuous export from Security Command Center to Pub/Sub. You notice that the Pub/Sub subscription has expired and no new findings have been delivered for over 31 days. You want to prevent this issue from recurring. What should you do?
column3: Configure a Cloud Scheduler job to send heartbeat messages to the Pub/Sub topic every 24 hours to keep the subscription active.
column4: Delete and recreate the NotificationConfig in SCC to refresh the connection between SCC and the Pub/Sub topic.
column5: Enable the SCC notification service account to automatically renew subscriptions by granting it the pubsub.subscriptions.update permission.
column6: Recreate the Pub/Sub subscription with the --expiration-period flag set to 'never' to prevent automatic expiration.
column8: By default, Pub/Sub subscriptions expire after 31 days of inactivity. Setting the --expiration-period flag to 'never' when creating the subscription ensures it does not automatically expire, which is critical for continuous security monitoring pipelines. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-enable-real-time-notifications

column2: You need to detect when Cloud KMS CryptoKey resources in your organization have a rotation period longer than 30 days, which violates your organization's internal compliance policy. The built-in Security Health Analytics detectors do not check for this specific rotation period threshold. You want to implement a detection that produces findings in Security Command Center. What should you do?
column3: Configure an Organization Policy constraint to enforce a maximum CryptoKey rotation period and rely on SCC posture management to detect violations.
column4: Create an Event Threat Detection custom module to monitor Cloud Audit Logs for CryptoKey operations with non-compliant rotation periods.
column5: Use the SCC API to create custom findings programmatically when a Cloud Function detects non-compliant CryptoKey configurations.
column6: Create a Security Health Analytics custom module that uses a CEL expression to check if the CryptoKey rotationPeriod property exceeds 30 days.
column8: Security Health Analytics custom modules allow you to define custom detection rules for misconfigurations that are not covered by built-in detectors. CEL expressions can evaluate resource properties like rotationPeriod against thresholds you specify, generating findings when the condition is met. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/custom-modules-sha-create

column2: Your organization's security operations team needs to create real-time security dashboards in Looker Studio to visualize Security Command Center (SCC) findings. The dashboards must display findings data that updates continuously as new security issues are detected. Which approach should you use to provide the data to Looker Studio?
column3: Use the SCC API to directly query findings from Looker Studio using a custom connector.
column4: Schedule bulk exports from SCC to BigQuery daily and connect Looker Studio to refresh the data source each morning.
column5: Export SCC findings to Cloud Storage as CSV files, and configure Looker Studio to use file upload data sources.
column6: Configure SCC continuous export to BigQuery, and connect Looker Studio to the BigQuery findings table.
column8: SCC continuous export streams new and updated findings to a BigQuery table in near real time. Looker Studio can then connect directly to this BigQuery table to create interactive visualizations that reflect the latest security findings. This is the recommended method for continuous data availability. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-analyze-findings-in-big-query

column2: Your security team is planning to enforce a new organization policy constraint that restricts the creation of external IP addresses on Compute Engine VMs. Before enforcing this policy in production, you need to understand its impact on existing resources and workloads without actually blocking any operations. What should you do?
column3: Create the organization policy at a folder level for non-production projects before applying it organization-wide.
column4: Create the organization policy using the dryRunSpec field to audit violations without enforcing the policy.
column5: Configure Cloud Monitoring alerts for the constraint and then enforce the policy immediately.
column6: Use Policy Simulator to test the constraint, then immediately enforce the policy at the organization level.
column8: An organization policy in dry-run mode logs violations as audit events without actually denying the violating actions. This allows you to understand the impact of the policy change over time before enforcing it in production. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/dry-run-policy
